#8973. Want to Ride More at Home? These 9 Stationary Bikes Make Training Easy, Quiet, and More Consistent

Find the right at-home ride, whether you want a budget spin bike or a premium smart-bike setup.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Weather and daylight don’t always cooperate with our riding schedules. And when we add work hours, family time, yardwork, and life’s daily grind, finding time to ride can feel impossible. Especially during the dark days of late autumn and winter, indoor riding becomes the only realistic option for many of us.

Luckily, indoor cycling is no longer the boring, arduous task it was only a decade ago. Today’s stationary bikes range from no-frills machines to fully connected setups. Some even feature live and on-demand classes, immersive virtual rides, and easy syncing with popular fitness platforms like Strava.

All of our editors and test team ride or train indoors for at least part of the year, sometimes even during the summer months to escape the heat. We’ve logged countless hours on stationary bikes and standard indoor trainers. In our testing, we’ve wrestled with finicky machines, endured glitchy interfaces and endless updates, and spent plenty of time grinding out virtual miles from our basements, garages, and home gyms; some of our editors have even taught spin classes.

Stationary bikes come in three main styles: Upright, recumbent, and dual-action. Upright models feel most like riding a traditional outdoor bike. Recumbent bikes offer a more reclined position, while dual-action bikes add upper-body work to the pedaling action.

Our testing and reviews focus on upright stationary bikes made by cycling-specific brands and general fitness companies. To differentiate between the two, we call models from fitness companies “exercise bikes” and those from cycling brands “indoor bikes” in this story.

Exercise bikes by fitness-oriented brands often feature a more upright riding position, multi-position handlebars with foam padding, and wide, comfort-style seats. The pedals usually have toe clips for use with running shoes.

Indoor bikes from traditional cycling brands typically mimic the body position, ride feel, and functional layout of outdoor bikes and feature dropbars, brake hoods, adjustable crank length, and narrow saddles. They usually feature high resistance for sprint workouts and virtual racing. These bikes used to be expensive, but prices have dropped over the last three years, making them a great choice for everyday indoor riders (not only hardcore enthusiasts).

The BowFlex C6 has the most capability at a reasonable price. High-quality and adjustable, this bike features Bluetooth connectivity so you can connect to apps like Peloton, Zwift, and Schwinn Trainer to join community rides and track progress.

The monitor displays time ridden, speed, mileage, heart rate, and resistance level. It doesn’t show wattage or precise RPM (it displays them on a scale). However, it does measure them, and you can see that data if you connect it to third-party training apps.

The flywheel is smooth and heavy, and you can crank the resistance up significantly through 100 incremental levels via a knob. Toe cages let you ride the C6 in regular running shoes or flip the pedals over and clip in with Shimano SPD cleats.

A great feature is the unit’s silence—you can use it day or night without waking your family. It comes with a forearm heart rate monitor and a pair of 3-pound dumbbells for light upper-body workouts while riding.

Want a more immersive experience? Check out BowFlex’s Velocore. It features a 22-inch integrated console with tons of class and entertainment streaming options, and is compatible with Zwift, Peloton, and JRNY.

If you don’t like traditional exercise bikes and want something that closely replicates the fit and feel of riding your actual bike, the Zwift Ride is an ideal solution—and the recently updated V2 model addresses issues our editors experienced with the first-gen model by adding adjustable crank length and saddle setback.

At its core, the Ride is an indoor cycling setup that eliminates the hassle of constantly mounting and unmounting your bike from a trainer or dedicating one bike solely for indoor use. The frame is exceptionally sturdy and has proven itself time and again under the stress of multiple test riders’ workouts. Paired with the reliable Kickr Core 2 trainer—our Best Overall smart trainer pick—the setup delivers a premium ride experience.

However, the real magic lies in its seamless integration with Zwift’s virtual world. You can join races, group rides, guided workouts, or explore immersive digital landscapes alongside fellow “Zwifters.” The most popular virtual cycling platform globally, Zwift succeeds by stripping away the monotony of indoor training. It gamifies the experience while offering social and competitive features that you can engage with as much—or as little—as you like.

The Schwinn IC4 is ideal if you want quick, easy access to ride metrics; you can see your data on the display—no subscription necessary. It also has a stand for your phone or tablet, USB charging for your devices, water bottle holders, and weights so everything you need is at your fingertips.

If you’re in the mood to be pumped up by a live class, Rouvy, or Zwift race, the Bluetooth option lets you jump right into third-party apps. The bike comes with a free two-month subscription to Schwinn’s platform, JRNY, which offers workout programming tailored to your preferences and over 200 virtual courses.

If you like the concept of the Zwift Ride but want an indoor bike with more adjustability and refinement, Wahoo’s Kickr Bike Shift is one of the best options. It’s essentially a stripped-down version of Wahoo’s super-premium, $4,000 Kickr Bike Pro; the Shift doesn’t include the Pro’s motor-electromagnetic resistance, gradient simulation, and some finishing details. While nifty features, they’re overkill for almost every indoor rider.

Like the Kickr Bike Pro, the Shift is quiet, super smooth, and easily adjustable to fit multiple users in a household. It also features standard bicycle component attachment. This makes it easy to replicate your outdoor bike’s fit on the Kickr Shift with your favorite saddle and handlebar. If you want the convenience and silence of an indoor bike, and a premium indoor riding setup, the Shift is the one to get.

Peloton redefined at-home fitness with its original bike—a sturdy, low-maintenance machine built to withstand years of sweaty daily rides. Its true draw, though, has always been Peloton’s vast library of on-demand and live classes, now spanning not only cycling but also running, core, and boot camp sessions. With the Peloton app, you can even take workouts on the go.

For years, the bike itself saw few changes—until the Bike+ arrived. It keeps the durable frame and quiet belt drive but adds a redesigned handlebar and a larger 23.8-inch touchscreen that rotates 360 degrees, making it easy to follow floor-based workouts. The model also features forward-facing Sonos-tuned speakers and auto-resistance that adjusts automatically to match instructor cues. Not everyone will use it, but those who do will love the convenience.

The most notable update is Peloton IQ: a built-in camera that tracks your movements, offers real-time feedback, and counts reps. There’s even a small fan above the screen for added comfort.

However, these upgrades come at a premium: the Bike+ is significantly more than the standard Peloton Bike. If you want to save $1,000, the standard Bike features solid build quality and full access to Peloton’s unmatched training ecosystem. But it doesn’t include auto-resistance, high-quality speakers, a rotating screen, Peloton IQ, a phone tray, and a fan.

This budget-priced, belt-driven bike features a 35-pound flywheel and provides a smooth, quiet ride. The resistance is adjustable with a knob regardless of pedaling speed. It also has an emergency brake that stops the flywheel immediately if necessary. According to Yosuda, the seat height adjusts to fit riders with inseams from 25 to 35 inches. Riders can also adjust the handlebar height and the fore-aft alignment of the padded saddle.

Although the Yosuda doesn’t connect to third-party sites, you can scroll through your time, speed, distance, and calories burned on the included single-button monitor. Below the monitor is a platform for a phone or tablet. The heavy-duty steel frame provides stability and durability, yet it’s easy to move thanks to the small wheels on the front edge.

If you’re spinning on a budget but want a connected experience, the Echelon EX-15 may be the stationary bike for you. This high-quality bike offers access to proprietary classes you can stream with an Echelon membership ($399.99 billed annually). Echelon’s membership isn’t limited to cycling content. The subscription offers rowing, running, strength training, yoga, and more. Enjoy workouts to music from artists including Pitbull and Lady Gaga—plus dance, EDM, hip hop, K-Pop, metal, Latin, and R&B.

The EX-15 bike itself is sized perfectly for smaller spaces, yet doesn’t skimp on comforts like an extra-large cushioned seat and padded handlebars. The mechanical knob lets you adjust resistance between 32 levels. You also get a free 30-day membership when you buy the EX-15 through Amazon.

It’s important to have one with solid construction and high weight capacity if you plan to put your stationary bike through the wringer. The Sunny Evolution Pro can withstand your most intense intervals and feels stable doing it. The 135-pound steel frame has a large footprint with leveling stabilizers in each corner to help prevent rocking.

Complementing that is a hefty 44-pound flywheel, which eliminates the inconsistent resistance you can feel near the top end of lighter wheels. The adjustable handlebar moves up and down and front to back, so you can dial in a position that's comfortable for your back, neck, and wrists.

The seat height accommodates riders with inseam lengths from 29 to 39 inches—a downside if you’re on the shorter side (Our 5-foot-2 barely made the cut, but awesome if you’re taller).

The Evolution Pro’s simplicity also makes it a great pick. Without Bluetooth connectivity (or even a monitor to display metrics), you can exercise without getting bogged down in numbers and be more in touch with your body at different PRE (perceived rate of exertion) levels.

The Keiser M3i is a studio-level spin bike with a clean, streamlined design and simplified interface. It has everything you need to nail your numbers in a hard workout, and then upload that data to apps like TrainingPeaks or Strava. The smooth flywheel is quiet, and its rear location means fewer sweat droplets land on it, so you can worry less about corrosion or wiping it down perfectly. The small monitor displays your power, cadence, time, gear, heart rate (if you’re wearing a connected strap), and total distance.

The media tray holds a phone or tablet above your handlebar so you can follow a route or guided workout as you ride, and it automatically uploads each effort in the included Keiser app to track your progress.

The saddle height adjustment uses preset stops; however, the wedge system lets you place the saddle in the precise spot you prefer. The looped handlebar is comfortable for a wide range of reaches, and the height adjustment accommodates riders as short as 4-foot-10 and as tall as 7 feet.

Stationary bikes come in three main options: upright, recumbent, and dual-action. The bikes recommended here are upright style, which puts you in a position that mimics how you’d sit on a traditional bicycle.

Recumbent exercise bikes seat you in a slightly reclined position with the pedals out in front of your hips rather than directly below, which can be easier on your back and neck. Dual-action exercise bikes have handlebars that move in and out, so riders incorporate their arms into the workout as they pedal.

Look for models with adjustable saddle height and position, plus adjustable handlebars. More adjustability makes it easier to find a comfortable riding position and get a good workout. Like a regular bicycle, a proper fit is crucial for the best experience. I like my indoor bike’s fit to match the position I ride outdoors.

All bikes feature bar-height adjustments, and some models let you adjust reach. Saddle height and setback adjustment options are also a must-have. They also have graduated markings, making it easier to get back to your preferred position after someone else uses the bike.

A dropbar offers hand positions that mimic road bikes, while a traditional bullhorn bar will be more familiar to those of you who frequent studio classes.

The two most common methods for regulating an indoor bike’s resistance are friction and magnets. Friction-based systems use leather or synthetic pads that press against a flywheel—It’s a simple, effective way to add precise, linear resistance. These resistance systems don’t require outside power to operate.

Magnetic resistance is quieter than friction systems. They use magnets (adjacent to the flywheel) to create an electric current that resists the wheel’s rotation. By increasing the current (strengthening the magnetic force), you have greater resistance. With no contact between the flywheel and magnets, this type of bike may offer a smoother ride than a friction-based one.

Some models use electromagnetic resistance controlled by software from a connected app. This allows platforms like Zwift to replicate hills and wind.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Bluetooth-equipped exercise bikes let you transmit your ride data directly to third-party training apps like Peloton or Zwift for in-ride metrics. If it has ANT+ capability, you can connect to extra sensors—like a cadence tracker or heart rate monitor—and display that data on your monitor or tablet. It’s not totally necessary for an interactive experience.

If you want to join virtual classes but aren’t sure which you’ll like (or you enjoy several), look for a bike with connectivity and media compatibility that lets you join the most platforms.

Bluetooth and ANT+ let you pair with training apps and sensors. If you use multiple apps, broad connectivity matters. Wi-Fi connectivity is nice to have if you plan to enter virtual races or use streaming-based setups.

Most indoor bikes function similarly; the accessories that set them apart. The most basic models are as simple as it gets, just an ergometer with a weighted flywheel and a pad to set resistance. At the other end of the spectrum are bikes like the Peloton, with elaborate software for recorded and live classes.

Decide how much technology you actually need for your indoor rides. Some cyclists want a feature-rich experience with training plans, classes, and group rides, while others want a stripped-down bike that covers the bare essentials.

Measure your available space before buying. If you will need to move it, also check the model’s weight and whether it has wheels.

Seat comfort matters; if possible, test-ride the seat that comes with your stationary bike before buying to make sure it's comfortable for you. Most stationary bikes come with a basic, comfort-style saddle. Models that allow you to swap the seat for aftermarket options offer more flexibility.

#8972. Unlock Your Full Potential by Fixing These Common Triathlon Body Imbalances

Triathletes can face muscle imbalances. These off-season exercises help build proper strength to prepare for next season. (Photo: Brad Kaminski/Triathlete)

Triathlon training is all about repetition, with hours upon hours spent catching and pulling in the pool, turning the pedals on the bike, and turning the legs over on the run. With that repetition comes natural imbalance, with some muscle groups getting overworked while others get neglected (or even weaken with age).

Over time, these imbalances can impact performance directly or indirectly by contributing to injury development. That’s why taking time to identify and address these imbalances now will help keep you healthy in the long run.

By pinpointing areas of weakness or asymmetry early on, athletes can target the stabilizing muscles, improve biomechanical efficiency across all three disciplines, and significantly reduce the risk of overuse injuries that often arise from repetitive strain. Here’s how.

While swimming is generally thought of as the “safest” discipline in triathlon, issues can and do occur, often manifesting as “swimmer’s shoulder.” Swimmer’s shoulder is a bit of a catch-all term for pain in the front of the shoulder that encompasses several pathologies, including rotator cuff issues.

Typically, underlying laxity and instability exist. One factor that can contribute to shoulder problems is a strength imbalance between the shoulder internal and external rotators, with the internal rotators becoming disproportionately strong in comparison to the external rotators. This makes sense, as the shoulder internal rotators are active throughout the catch and pull, working to rotate the arm in and push against water.

But the external rotators still play an important role, as they help to stabilize the shoulder joint, keeping the ball of the joint centered in the socket to help prevent impingement and pain with overhead use and shoulder abnormalities. To decrease injury risk, external rotators should have about two-thirds of the strength of the internal rotators.

The most reliable, valid ways to check this involve specialized dynamometry equipment that measures force. But if you’re just looking to get a general idea, check how many reps of each of the below motions you can do until fatigue.

In this case, the test (lying prone, rotating the back of the arm up) can also be used as an effective strengthening exercise for external rotation. Start with higher reps, lower weights to learn the motion (3 sets of 10-12), then work up to higher weights, lower reps (4 sets of 6-8) to build more strength.

If this position causes pain or is too difficult at first, a side-lying shoulder external rotation is also a good option.

While the incidence of overuse injuries attributed to cycling is generally lower than those attributed to running, they can and do occur, most commonly impacting the knee and lower back. Although singling out contributing factors is difficult, the prolonged posture and muscle activations associated with cycling predispose athletes to overdeveloped quadriceps and an undeveloped posterior chain (glutes, hamstrings, back extensors) and lateral hip muscles.

Cyclists need strong quads – these are the predominant muscle used to power the pedal stroke. But the glutes and hamstrings do assist, so neglecting those leaves some power on the table. Plus, that injury-prone lower back needs adequate strength and endurance to withstand hours spent in a forward-flexed position.

Also, because muscle weakness and tightness often go hand-in-hand, related limitations in mobility throughout the posterior chain limit a cyclist’s ability to comfortably hold more aggressive aero positions. Those quads of steel will only help so much if you’re sitting up to ease back and glute discomfort by the end of a long ride!

The strength and endurance of the posterior chain (and also the lateral hip, which can play a role when it comes to knee pain on the bike) can be checked using a single-leg bridge hold.

The single-leg RDL is a good choice for eliciting both high force and stretch in the hamstrings and strengthening the gluteal muscles, back extensors, and lateral hips. Isolating each leg can also help with side-to-side imbalances.

When it comes to muscle strength and running, the glutes have been frequently implicated as the cause of (and solution to) many issues. But, while the glutes do play an important stability-related role in the run gait and deficits have been linked with injury, the true workhorse of the run gait – the calves – often gets overlooked and under-strengthened.

The soleus (one of the calf muscles) experiences forces of up to eight times body weight and produces up to 50% of forward propulsive power while running. Because the calves insert onto the heel via the Achilles tendon (which acts as a spring during running), the two are linked, with decreased calf strength seen in athletes with Achilles issues compared to healthy controls.

Strong calves can also help to protect against tibial bone stress injuries. Masters athletes lose calf strength (and Achilles tendon stiffness) disproportionately to other muscle groups with age, leading to both a reduction in propulsion and step length and an increased risk of lower leg soft tissue injuries such as strains and tendinopathies. So, when it comes to both performance and helping to guard against many common lower leg injuries, first check the powerhouse muscles below the knee!

Calf strength can be tested with a single-leg calf raise test.

The test here can again be used as the exercise – just load it up!

So, while the different disciplines and repeated motions of triathlon might lend athletes to certain imbalances, not all is lost! Triathletes can make themselves stronger, more resilient, and faster with some awareness and work – so don’t neglect those details.

#8971. Garmin’s New Screen-Free Fitness Band Takes Aim at WHOOP and Oura With No Subscription Required

The CIRQA band tracks a broad sweep of daily health and fitness metrics, giving Garmin users a fuller view of life on and off the bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Most fitness trackers come with a second price tag: a monthly fee for seeing the data they collect. Garmin’s $200 CIRQA Smart Band needs no subscription for core health, sleep, and activity tracking. That sets it apart from WHOOP’s and Oura’s paid membership models. Garmin’s pitch is straightforward: buy the band, wear it around the clock, and check the data in Garmin Connect without another recurring bill. It’s a refreshing proposition in a world lousy with subscriptions.

Very basically, the CIRQA is a screen-free fabric band designed for all-day wear on the wrist or upper arm; the concept is similar to the Whoop band. It tracks heart rate, sleep, HRV, stress, skin temperature, Pulse Ox, and Garmin’s Body Battery estimate. Garmin claims up to 10 days of battery life. The band supports more than 80 activity types, uses your phone for GPS, and can broadcast heart rate to a cycling computer. Garmin pitches the lack of a screen as a feature for riders who want the data but don’t want to wear a smartwatch.

The single button handles one favorite activity, which you set in Garmin Connect. Press it once to start recording and again to stop; the band vibrates and flashes an LED to confirm. You can start other activities in the app, and CIRQA can automatically detect some sessions from movement and exertion data. That keeps the band clean and simple, with setup and seeing the details handled through the phone.

I’ve tracked rides with cycling computers since the days of the fabled Garmin Edge 500. Over the years, I’ve sent those files through Strava, TrainingPeaks, and a rotating cast of other platforms. Plenty of them can tell me what I did on the bike. Garmin’s appeal, and maybe its best selling point, is the Garmin Connect app.

With a Garmin cycling computer, your ride data already lives in Garmin Connect. Add the CIRQA, or another Garmin wearable, and the app puts that training alongside sleep, stress, HRV, and other health metrics. The CIRQA’s unique appeal isn’t any one metric the band collects. It’s that those metrics feed into the same ecosystem as your ride data, giving you a more complete picture of your training in the full context of your day.

That can be useful if you’re trying to make better training decisions yourself, or if you work with a coach who wants more context than your power files and weekly mileage can provide. A hard workout looks different after a great night’s sleep than it does after a week of poor sleep and high stress. Putting that data in one place makes it easier to see when a planned session fits or when it's time to adjust the plan.

Wearable device options are more plentiful than ever, and the CIRQA won’t be the right pick for everyone. Its clearest audience is the rider who already uses Garmin Connect and wants health and recovery data alongside cycling workouts. If your bike computer already uploads rides there, the CIRQA adds context about what happens between them. That connection is the main reason to choose it.

It should also appeal to people who want to track sleep, stress, and activity without taking on another subscription. You don’t need a paid membership for CIRQA’s core tracking, which makes it a good option for riders who want to monitor their daily data without another recurring bill.

The other clear fit is someone who wants less screen time on their wrist. The CIRQA has no display or smartwatch notifications. Maybe you wear an analog watch and want to keep it that way; maybe you’re tired of your smartwatch and want a wearable that quietly collects data for you to check later. If you want live metrics and notifications or even the time at a glance, the CIRQA probably isn’t for you.

Sleep tracking and HRV status worked seamlessly for me. I don’t find much value in comparing one wearable’s numbers directly with another’s. It’s more important for the numbers to be consistent and CIRQA’s were. Its readings tracked with how I felt from one day to the next, and also mirrored the trend lines of numbers from other smartwatches I’ve been testing, which made them useful as context rather than scores I had to chase.

Having sleep, HRV, and stress inside Garmin Connect alongside my ride data made those numbers actionable for me. I’m self-coached, so I’m deciding every day whether to do the workout on my calendar, go easier, or take a day off. Garmin Connect’s ability to bring my on-bike training and the rest of my day together in one place felt like the most useful thing about the CIRQA band.

The band has a single button, an underrated feature, and maybe a Band-Aid, too. I liked being able to start and stop an activity manually instead of hoping the band’s auto-detection caught it, especially for commutes, hikes, and runs. In general, auto-detection did a good job with walks, runs, hikes, gym workouts, and swims. My twice-a-day e-bike daycare trip was a different story: CIRQA picked it up about half the time. If it were more consistent on those rides, the button would matter less. But even if automatic activity tracking worked perfectly, having a manual stop/start button feels useful.

As someone trying to avoid another subscription, I see CIRQA as Garmin’s best alternative to WHOOP. There’s meaningful overlap in the day-to-day metrics, like sleep and HRV. WHOOP packages those metrics more neatly into an easy-to-read Strain/Recovery dashboard. CIRQA’s advantage is the Garmin Connect app, which combines ride data with all the metrics CIRQA tracks, which makes it an easy sell for existing Garmin users. But its lack of a subscription makes it easy to recommend to everyone else looking for a wearable device.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8970. 11-Minute Stretch and Breathwork Routine to Soothe Your System

Radiance Basden is a certified yoga teacher and passionate advocate for stress reduction, mental resilience, and restorative wellness. Here, she guides readers through a gentle movement and breathwork practice that’s even better when done outside.

It’s a beautiful day to breathe on purpose.

Incorporating grounding practices—including breathing exercises, yoga, and mindful stretching—into your daily routine is one of the the simplest ways to teach your body that it’s okay to relax.

If you have the opportunity to do this sort of breathwork outdoors, the experience can be even more beneficial. When I need to regain my equilibrium, I spend time in nature. After all, outdoor spaces are scientifically proven to soothe your system. Listen to the sounds, notice the world around you, breathe in the fresh air, and embrace the power of simple movements done with intention. You’ll be surprised by how quickly you can come back to yourself.

Begin in a comfortable seat, preferably on the edge of something supportive, whether a chair, couch, bench, even a rock. Place your feet flat on the ground. Both before you start and throughout your practice, check in with yourself and make sure that your shoulders, face, and hands are relaxed.

Rest your hands on your knees—palms facing up to receive energy, facing down for extra grounding. If you feel called to do so, gently close your eyes. Start with 3 deep breaths, slowly inhaling through your nose, slowly exhaling through your mouth.

Now, it’s time to bring in humming breath. Inhale through your nose, and as you exhale, make a humming sound. Continue to hum for the entire length of your exhalation, however long that might be.

Repeat this 5 times or however many you’d like.

Take 3 deep breaths, allowing yourself to sit in stillness while mentally checking in with your body.

Can you still feel the vibrations of your humming?

Make sure your feet are planted about shoulder’s-width distance apart. When you’re ready, begin to move through some hip circles. Circle toward the right, leading with your shoulders and guiding your torso forward, around, and back.

When you’re ready, switch directions and enjoy 8 more circles.

As you move through your hip circles, pay attention to any parts of your body that feel particularly tense or tight and spend some time there. Pause to rock, deepen your stretch, or bring in whatever movement or breath you might need to relax the area.

Next, embody your breath with a seated flow through Cat-Cow. With your inhalation, arch your back and lift your chin toward the sky, bringing your hands to rest on the sides of your hips in a seated variation of Cow Pose.

With your exhalation, round your spine and tuck your chin and bring your hands to rest on the front of your knees in a seated variation of Cat Pose.

Repeat this pattern of movement 10 times, moving with the pace of your own breath.

With your next exhalation, clasp your hands and extend your arms forward in a variation of Seated Forward Bend.

Take 1 full breath here before inhaling your arms up to the sky and exhaling them down at your sides.

Stand up and prepare for a variation of Breath of Joy. Inhale through your nose to throw your arms up overhead, taking a slight backbend in the process.

Exhale through your mouth, making a whooshing sound. Bend forward, bend your knees, and throw your arms back behind you.

Repeat this pattern of movement for 1 full minute.

With you next exhalation, come into Mountain Pose. Stand tall here for 5 cycles of breath through your nose.

Now, for your last bit of breathwork, take 3 more slow breaths, inhaling through your nose and exhaling through your mouth.

#8969. The Biomechanics of Speed: How Your Form Can Improve Your Pace

This “speedwork” is way more fun than sprint repeats.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Whether you’re lacing up your shoes for a 5K or gearing up for a longer endurance race, if you want to get faster, you have to do both longer runs and speedwork sessions to train your aerobic and anaerobic systems. But for the biggest speed gains, you should also look beyond your cardiovascular fitness and work your… posture?

“People often think of running as a lower body sport, but running is everything going on between your ears and everywhere below,” says Anh Bui, D.P.T., C.S.C.S., a former collegiate runner, doctor of physical therapy, and biomechanics specialist in Oakland, California.

While you probably can’t (and shouldn’t) transform your running form into the stride of, say, Olympians on the podium, you can incorporate tweaks to make your mechanics more ideal for you. And that can help you improve performance, get faster, and lower your risk of getting hurt.

“There’s high variability between everyone’s biomechanics based on how you’re structurally and genetically built,” says Bui. “The key is to optimize movement, not force idealism, and to run efficiently to maximize speed and minimize injury risk.”

Read on for more about how each part of your biomechanics, from head to toe, contributes to your speed—plus a handful of moves to add to your routine that’ll help you pick up the pace.

It’s easier to maintain good posture on a short jog versus a long training run when your body starts to drag. But focusing on staying tall and keeping your shoulders from slumping is an important part of efficient running form—not to mention makes it easier to breathe.

Standing up straight as you run with a slight forward lean helps pull you forward, says Ellen Foster, D.P.T., a doctor of physical therapy, movement quality expert, and running coach in Cincinnati. “I like to encourage runners to sort of ‘fall’ forward from the ankles so that their hips are slightly in front of their feet,” she says. “Just make sure you don’t lean forward by bending at the hips or waist, as that would lead to pushing your hips back and losing valuable hip extension.”

Your arms play a surprisingly big role in picking up your pace. Just try pumping your arms harder next time you’re huffing up a hill and see how much it helps. Here’s why: The motion of your arms and legs are linked. “And our arms act as pendulums to help balance our trunk, as forces travel up our body from our legs,” says Foster. “So, when we swing our arms in a more efficient way, our legs often follow their lead.”

While research on just how crucial the arm swing is to running mechanics is limited (most studies focus more on the lower half of the body), and results offer mixed information, most researchers agree that swinging the arms helps with vertical oscillation (or how much we move upward as we stride), side-to-side balance, and minimizing rotation.

“Anecdotally, I find that arm swing drills can be a good starting place when working on increasing cadence, especially if someone is struggling to increase cadence due to poor coordination,” Foster says. Cadence, or the number of steps you take per minute, often changes depending on the speed you’re running, but experts suggest a quicker cadence can limit overstriding and help with forward momentum.

Sprinters tend to drive their knees up aggressively, about 90 degrees from the ground. That’s not sustainable over longer distances, says Bui, who says distance runners should ideally maintain more like 45 degrees of knee drive.

Why does the position of your knees matter? “Picking up your speed without appropriate knee drive will increase likelihood of overstriding, or landing with the foot far in front of your body,” Bui explains. That can slow you down and increases ground reaction forces—or forces exerted by the ground onto the body, Bui says—and ups your chances of injury.

When considering how your feet play into your form and your pace, a lot of it is about those ground reaction forces. If you reduce the time your feet come in contact with the ground, you can potentially lower the force on your body—and lessen your risk of injuries like shin splints, says Foster.

“When we look at vertical ground reaction forces (vGRF) across time, midfoot striking has a lower rate of vGRF with one smooth peak,” Bui explains. By contrast, heel striking has a longer ground contact time, leading to a higher peak force and greater load on the body. This is because your ankle dorsiflexors (when you pull toes toward shins) can’t efficiently absorb the impact of your foot strike, and therefore, your knee joint takes on extra force, she adds.

Try to pick up your cadence and adjust so you’re striking the ground with your foot underneath your body (rather than out too far in front) to help reduce those forces up the leg. Typically, heel striking accompanies overstriding—which can increase risk of injury from the added load—and upping your cadence can help you avoid it.

Keep in mind that your body needs time to adjust to any changes you make in your form. Also, while your body may take on more force with a heel strike, it doesn’t always lead to more injuries or slower speeds. It’s one piece of the biomechanical puzzle. “Heel striking isn’t inherently dangerous by itself,” Foster says.

To improve your biomechanics, working with a run-form coach or physical therapist with advanced training in motor learning or neuromuscular re-education is hugely beneficial, says Foster. “It’s easy to understand the correct biomechanics, but it’s much more challenging to implement them,” she says.

Although working with one of these pros is ideal, a few exercises you can practice on your own can help you get a jumpstart on improving biomechanics.

Here are five biomechanical drills that focus on different aspects of your form. Do them often (for a few minutes as part of your warmup before every run, for example) to make the movements feel like second nature. Then, when you’re working to incorporate tweaks to your form into your run, don’t try to make several changes all at once; try sprinkling them into your runs slowly, thinking about a single form tweak for 30 seconds once per mile.

Just make sure not to jump in too quickly. All tweaks to your body’s biomechanics should be gradual or you risk the chance of injury, says Foster.

Why it works: This super-quick drill emphasizes balance and stability while firing up your posterior chain, which helps develop a more powerful push-off.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Raise right knee to hip height. In a quick, explosive movement, lower right foot to floor and raise left knee high, then lower left knee and raise right knee to hip height again. Do 5 reps. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: Practicing this movement at a quick, consistent pace helps make your arm swing more efficient.

How to do it: Set a metronome app (like Metronome Beats) to a beats per minute that feels in sync with your running cadence; 180 bpm is ideal but dial it back if that feels too quick. Sitting on the edge of a chair or standing with feet hip-width apart, pump arms forward and back to the beat, starting with 10-15 seconds. Do 3-5 sets, resting for about 10-20 second between sets.

Why it works: The plyometric motion of this jump helps prep your tendons to store and release energy quickly. Start by doing the move with both legs, then progress to one leg at a time, recommends Bui.

How to do it: Stand with feet hip-width apart. Keeping legs straight, push off the floor from the ball of feet and swing arms up to jump as high as you can. As soon as you land, jump again. Do 5 reps, jumping as quickly as you can (and minimizing your feet’s contact with the floor). Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Why it works: This quick movement increases tendon capacity, trains your body to absorb load as you make contact with the ground, and decreases the time your feet stay in contact with the ground.

How to do it: Stand on the edge of a step or box about a foot tall. With right foot leading, step both feet down to floor. As soon as left foot hits floor, jump up explosively, pushing off floor with both feet. Repeat for 5 steps. Then repeat with left foot leading the step down. Do 2 sets.

Why it works: This move is really just running, with exaggerated motions that mimic ideal sprinting form—and helps develop speed, power, and explosiveness.

How to do it: On a track or long patch of ground, jog forward with as long a stride as possible. As you move, raise the front knee as high as possible while lifting the back foot (keeping leg straight) behind you. Continue for 10 reps total. Rest for 1-2 minutes, then repeat for a second set.

Recommended Experience: No experience necessary! Anyone can accomplish this training plan.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: This plan is for a new runner who is just getting back into exercise.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a new runner who has been exercising regularly for at least a year, or someone who has completed a few 5Ks or 10Ks and can complete 6 miles in one workout. This plan peaks at 28 miles in a week with a 12-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For runners comfortable exercising for at least an hour at a moderate effort. This plan peaks at 32 miles in a week with a 14-mile long run.

Get the PlanRecommended Experience: For a consistent runner used to regularly working out four to five times a week. The plan starts with a 10-mile long run and peaks at 44 to 47 miles a week with a 22-mile long run, helping you average under a 9:10 per mile come race day.

#8968. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K

Learn how to tackle the approachable distances with the power of walk breaks.

You’ve completed your Magic Mile time trials, dialed in your pacing, and tracked your progress with your run/walk workouts. Now, it’s time to hit the starting line!

The 5K and 10K make for perfect race distances for beginner and veteran run/walkers alike. Whether you’re shooting to cross your first finish line or earn that big PR, you can train for and race toward your goals with the run/walk method powering every step.

The Runner’s World guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, helps you get to the finish line and cover two of the most popular and approachable distances. Pair our chapter with one of our dedicated training plans to prepare for your first or fastest 5K or 10K yet.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a 5K & 10K, we’ll teach you:

Training Principles for Consistent Success

For beginners, a 5K or 10K serves as a great introduction to using the run/walk training strategy for race day. It’s an opportunity to get accustomed to pacing, structure your intervals, and follow a dedicated run/walk training plan. Once you’ve nailed your 5K/10K training block, you may find it easier to bump up to longer distances and chase after new race goals.

But even if you’re not a racing newcomer, a shorter, approachable distance can be an ideal place to start with run/walk. You might even race faster with the run/walk method than you did previously when running the entire distance.

The shorter the distance, the shorter the walk break will likely be, especially if you’re shooting for a PR. Use your data from your Magic Mile test to determine your goal pace for race day.

Some crucial benefits of using run/walk for a 5K/10K include:

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 6-8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 5Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (2 easy runs, 1 long run), 1 easy walk day, 2 strength train days, 2 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 30-minute run/walk + strength trainingRecommended Experience: For new runners and those who have been running for three months and are ready to do their first race.

Weekly Schedule: 3 total run/walk days (1 race rehearsal, 1 speed workout, 1 long run), 2 strength train days, 3 rest or cross-train daysSample Workout: 8 x 400-meter repeatsRecommended Experience: For an experienced runner, who has done 10Ks and/or half marathons or marathons, and wants to use the run/walk method to get faster.

With one of Runner’s World’s dedicated 5K and 10K run/walk training plans, you can build your endurance and speed for tackling your race. Spanning anywhere from six to eight weeks, our plans include three run/walk days, two to three rest or cross-train days, and even additional easy walk and strength training days, depending on the plan. Whether you’re a beginner looking to dip your toes in run/walk or an experienced run/walker chasing after a personal best, we have a plan tailored to your goals.

Newcomers embarking on their run/walk journey for the first time can also utilize our Couch to 5K training plan. It’s a 10-week plan with two to three days of run/walk, two days of rest, and two days of strength training, aimed at getting you across your first finish line.

#8967. COROS Doubled the Price of Its Bike Computer. Can the DURA 2 Compete With Premium Rivals?

COROS kept the feature that made the original stand out and rebuilt nearly everything around it. Now the DURA 2 has to justify its place among other premium options.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

The original COROS DURA stood out for two reasons: battery life and price. At $249, it was a (relatively) affordable alternative to the Garmin and Wahoo computers most riders already knew. Just with a solar charging feature that made charging almost optional. But it also felt like the first-generation product that it was. The DURA 2 is COROS’s attempt to move beyond that niche and compete with computers from Garmin, Wahoo, and Hammerhead.

The DURA 2 has a new, unusually slim form factor, a larger 3.5-inch touchscreen, updated maps, and redesigned controls that replace the original’s thumb dial. It also adds voice commands, music controls, and a built-in bike bell. The screen is a memory-in-pixel display, rather than the bright, phone-like panel found on OLED displays on the Karoo and latest Garmin head units. COROS’s priority here is a legible readout while minimizing the power demand of the screen.

Battery life remains the headline. COROS rates the DURA 2 for up to 120 hours in standard GPS mode, or 70 hours with dual-frequency GPS, before factoring in solar charging. After 30 hours of riding with paired sensors, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness, my unit still had 77 percent battery remaining.

The price of the DURA 2 has changed along with the ambition. The computer costs $499 on its own, or $549 with COROS’s aluminum mount—a steep jump from the original, though you can skip the bundled mount if you already have a compatible one. The question is whether the DURA 2’s much longer battery life, improved interface, and the COROS ecosystem make it a compelling alternative at this price. After riding it, I think the new DURA is a much more complete and compelling computer. But it hasn’t quite closed the gap to its competitors.

The DURA 2’s memory-in-pixel screen won't win anyone over with vivid colors or smartphone-like detail. That’s fine with me. I don’t use a cycling computer to watch videos or scroll social media. I want to glance down, find the information I need, and get back to riding. The DURA 2 does that well, with arguably the most legible screen in direct sunlight I’ve seen.

The screen struggles most in inconsistent, high-contrast light, such as bright dappled sunlight through tree cover. This is when I wish the DURA 2 offered any kind of meaningful backlight. To my eyes, changing the screen brightness from full to all the way off made no noticeable difference. This wasn’t a huge issue on basic numerical data pages, which stayed very legible, but when you’re trying to discern map detail, it felt a little tough, especially while riding.

Some riders will still prefer the brighter, higher-resolution screens on the Hammerhead Karoo or Garmin’s high-end computers. That’s a valid preference. How beautiful a screen looks isn’t a huge priority for me.

The maps themselves are a big improvement over the original DURA. In my experience, the Hammerhead is still the standard for map legibility and ease of on-device navigation, but the DURA 2 is now quite good. It shows street names at closer zoom levels, and the map responds quickly when you pan or zoom. Both the processing speed and touchscreen response are dramatically better than on the first DURA, and are now close to what I expect from Garmin and Hammerhead.

One screen quirk is that Coros has no way to manually lock the screen. COROS says it will automatically lock when it detects too much rain. I would still like to have a manual lock setting, even if the automatic system works as promised. I suspect COROS could add that option in a future firmware update.

Good riddance to the dial. I gave the original DURA’s dial a fair chance, and it could be useful once I got used to it, especially with gloves. But I also found it clunky and a pain to use while riding. The DURA 2’s new haptic buttons work as advertised, and the touchscreen is far more responsive than it was on the original.

The screen is a little less responsive with gloves on, but not dramatically less than other touchscreens I’ve used. The physical buttons help, and the new layout feels more straightforward. The DURA 2 is simply easier to operate on the bike compared to the original.

The offset Garmin-style mount connection is a small but useful design feature. Larger computers can run into clearance problems with some proprietary out-front mounts. Because the DURA 2’s connection point sits farther back, I’m less concerned about that here. I tested the computer without buying COROS’s optional mount, which I appreciate having as an option because I already have a bin full of included out-front mounts that I couldn’t give away if I tried. Being able to opt out of yet another one was actually kind of refreshing.

I’ve recorded 31 hours of riding on the DURA 2, and the battery is still at 82.4%. That’s with multiple sensors paired, occasional navigation, and the screen at full brightness.

Even with the caveat that battery usage will vary from user to user based on factors like location and use case, the battery performance is extraordinary. If you regularly do rides longer than 20 hours, this is probably the computer to get. No other current head unit I’ve tested comes close to this kind of real-world endurance.

For shorter rides, the advantage is less dramatic but still useful: charging becomes one less thing to remember. And Coros deserves kudos here for maintaining battery-life performance with the DURA 2 while adding a larger screen and more processing power to the unit.

Navigation on the DURA 2 with the updated maps is a clear improvement. The faster processor makes the device feel much less sluggish when zooming or scrolling the map, and the map is easy to read while riding. Street names at tighter zoom levels are a welcome addition compared to what the original DURA offered.

My main reservation is that rerouting still depends on your phone. I get the practical argument: most of us ride with a phone anyway, and the phone can handle it. But it still feels like a shortcoming in a $500 cycling computer. Other units can reroute on their own, and I’d rather not rely on a Bluetooth phone connection when I’ve already paid for a dedicated device.

The rerouting itself is kind of hit or miss. Most of my testing has been in Southeastern Pennsylvania, and so far the DURA 2 (or, I guess I should say, the Coros app on my phone) has sent me down a trail into a stream crossing on my commuter bike only once. Following a route I designed and loaded onto the DURA 2 has gone smoothly, as expected. But I wouldn’t trust the Coros-suggested routes when navigating to a point on a map or when rerouting in an unfamiliar place.

Finally, I personally don’t mind manually loading a route onto my head unit. But in 2026, route sync should be mostly automatic. Hopefully, they can add that in a future firmware update.

Sensor pairing and ride syncing have been trouble-free for me. I’ve had no issues with the sensors I use, and activities push to the app smoothly after a ride. Which is what I expect from a core cycling computer function in 2026.

Structured training is now more than passable. I don’t use my head unit to guide workouts, but I appreciate that COROS has made the feature more useful for riders who do. You can now pause an interval without pausing the ride recording, which feels like it should have been possible from the start, but I’m always happy to see improvements.

The COROS app and Training Hub are also strengths. In some ways, the experience is simpler than Garmin Connect, and I find parts of it easier to use. You can build routes, send rides to Strava and other platforms, and see your training data alongside recovery information from a COROS watch. If you already wear a COROS watch off the bike, that integration is useful. As with Garmin Connect, though, you get the most from the system when you use the company’s hardware.

The new music controls are great, and they’re seamlessly integrated. The electronic bell sounds like an actual bike bell, which is great. But it can’t currently be paired to a bonus button on Di2 or AXS, which Coros can fix in a future firmware update.

The voice control is puzzling to me. Garmin just unveiled this feature on its latest 1060 unit, and I’m just not sure why. I’ve spent 20 years riding without talking to my cycling computer. I would much rather companies perfect their UI and button interfaces so riders can quickly and simply access the functions they need instead of implementing voice controls. I’m sure some riders will find it useful, but I can’t see myself talking to my cycling computer any time soon. Especially since every time I tried to talk to the DURA 2 while riding, it couldn’t understand me, so there's definitely room for improvement.

The DURA 2 is a much better computer than the original DURA. It has a better screen, faster maps, more responsive controls, usable training features, and a more complete app experience. Most importantly, it keeps the exceptional battery life that made the original interesting in the first place.

The price has doubled, and there's really no getting around that. I think the improvements, plus the new form factor, justify an increase. But at $499, the DURA 2 is basically the same price as the Hammerhead Karoo 3 and not much cheaper than the Garmin Edge 850. Both units have their own strengths and trade-offs, but they're polished and fully functional. By contrast, I have written the phrase “hopefully this gets fixed in a future firmware update” three times in this review.

The DURA 2’s biggest strength is that it no longer feels like a budget computer asking you to overlook its rough edges. It feels like a serious head unit with exceptional battery life, and if you regularly ride 20 hours straight, it’s the easy pick. If you don’t, the DURA 2 is still a big step forward over the original, but the rough edges still need a bit more sanding given the jump in asking price.

Test Editor Dan Chabanov got his start in cycling as a New York City bike messenger but quickly found his way into road and cyclocross racing, competing in professional cyclocross races from 2009 to 2019 and winning a Master’s National Championship title in 2018. Prior to joining Bicycling in 2021, Dan worked as part of the race organization for the Red Hook Crit, as a coach with EnduranceWERX, as well as a freelance writer and photographer.

#8966. Tracksmith Created the Blueprint for Indie Running Brands. Can It Survive Without Its Architect?

The Boston-born apparel company enters a new era following the sudden departure of founder Matt Taylor.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

The running journalist Mario Fraioli still remembers the shorts Matt Taylor sent him in 2014, when Taylor was launching a new apparel brand.

Dubbed the Longfellow short, the prototype pair had a button at the waist, they were longer than typical running shorts, and they didn’t have a liner. The idea was, in Fraioli’s telling, that you could go straight from an easy run to a coffee shop and still look presentable. Taylor wanted to know what Fraioli thought.

Fraioli’s reaction? He didn’t love them. The sizing was off for him.

He was, however, intrigued by Taylor’s passion for the apparel and the nascent brand.

“He was super excited,” Fraioli told Runner’s World.

With $35,000 of his savings from a previous endeavor and seed round capital, Taylor launched Tracksmith later in 2014. The initial product line was four men’s items, including those Longfellow shorts and a “Grayboy” T-shirt that mimicked the standard-issue shirt of college athletic departments, plus a spike bag and Meter magazine. Women’s clothing followed about nine months later.

The idea of Tracksmith? Top-quality running apparel for people who were not professional athletes, but trained hard and loved their sport. The names and designs of the products reflected the roots of the sport and Taylor’s reverence for its history.

Frugal runners initially had sticker shock. Tracksmith manufactured its clothing in the U.S., using quality materials, which cost more. But the company was one of the earliest independent running brands selling apparel for serious runners outside of the major shoe companies. Women’s running apparel brand Oiselle had hatched earlier, in 2007.

Tracksmith quickly grew. It added retail locations in Boston and New York, and hundreds of items for sale—including four shoe styles, which were added in 2022.

Now, Taylor has been abruptly pushed out of the company he founded, and industry observers are left wondering if the brand can keep growing without him.

Fraioli, who is now a coach and writer of the Morning Shakeout newsletter, announced the news of Taylor’s departure in his October 13 email, writing that the newsletter would no longer have Tracksmith as a sponsor.

“A big part of my belief in Tracksmith was tied to my belief in Matt’s character, authenticity, and creative vision, and with him gone, I’ve lost confidence in where the brand is headed,” he wrote.

It’s unclear what precipitated the split. Taylor declined to speak to Runner’s World, and former employees were in the dark about the details of his ouster.

Taylor had hired a CEO in January, Jared Carver, a veteran of Converse, to handle the day-to-day operations so he could get back to focusing on the “brand’s vision and creative expression,” according to a company LinkedIn post eight months ago.

In a concurrent post, Taylor wrote: “I didn’t start Tracksmith to be a CEO—I started it to change the way running is presented with the hope of changing how it is perceived. My goals were to build distinct products, tell compelling stories and create a sense of camaraderie, the same you might feel on your cross country team.”

Insiders and one analyst painted a picture of a brand that opened a lane for rival independent retailers to follow suit—and perhaps surpass—Tracksmith. Bandit and Satisfy are two of the brands frequently cited as competitors, especially as the sport has seen enormous growth coming out of COVID.

“Other people have, I think, drafted on their success and made the marketplace more competitive,” said Matt Powell, an industry analyst who is a senior advisor with BCE Consulting. “For any brand, I think it’s hard to stay ahead of the trends, and you never have an unassailable position. Somebody’s always trying to copy you, or do what you do better. That's a big challenge for a small brand.”

It is not known if Tracksmith was profitable, as the company is privately held, and those who were close to Taylor in the company’s early days wondered whether investors and board members were growing impatient. Tracksmith would not talk about the company’s financials or name the members of its board. A Tracksmith representative confirmed Taylor’s exit and that of Matt Pauk, the head of product, who left in August, and offered a statement:

“Matt Taylor, Tracksmith’s founder, has transitioned out of his role with the company and departed Tracksmith. Matt’s unique vision created the Tracksmith we know today, and undoubtedly shaped the culture and business of running. At its core, Tracksmith has always been about people—our team, our partners, the people who push the sport forward, and the runners we serve. These values remain unchanged, and we are confident in our ability to continue building upon the strong foundation established in Tracksmith's 12 years.”

As early employees try to process what happened, they expressed appreciation for what Taylor brought to the industry.

Taylor, they said, was the animating force of the brand. He named the various products after runners in history, and arranged artful photo shoots with athletes in the mist and the mud. His love of the sport was obvious. (He’s still a serious runner. In 2024, Taylor ran the Boston Marathon, at age 47, in 2:43:18.)

Lou Serafini was one of the first employees. Like Fraioli, he didn’t immediately get what the brand was about. At the time, he was working at Heartbreak Hill Running Company before Taylor recruited him to work for Tracksmith.

“I remember being kind of confused,” Serafini said, “not really understanding what they were trying to do. I think most visionary brands have a little bit of that, where it has to be different enough where it makes people kind of scratch their head a little bit.”

Serafini went to Tracksmith’s first Boston Marathon pop-up in 2015, in an empty storefront at 285 Newbury Street, which in 2017 became its permanent home, just blocks from the marathon finish line. (Now pop-ups are a standard part of major marathons with cutting-edge brands; expos are in dreary convention centers, a necessary stop for runners to make to pick up their bibs.)

Serafini’s first job was managing the shop and building a running community there. “That was the first time where I really realized the ethos of the brand,” he said.

When he first started at Tracksmith in 2017, if Serafini saw any runners wearing Tracksmith clothing along the Charles River paths, it was an exciting moment. By the end of his tenure, in 2024, he remembered spotting runners in the brand all over the world.

The best days at Tracksmith always have been Boston Marathon Monday and the Tuesday after. Runners would crowd the shop, pick up a free poster, and get it stamped with their finishing time. “The focus of those days was to sit in the track house and stamp posters and have a 30-second conversation with somebody about how their race went,” Serafini said. In 2018, the year Boston went off in a nor’easter, the Tracksmith headquarters on Newbury became a hospital of sorts for runners trying to get warm.

Two other former employees, in conversations with Runner’s World, echoed Serafini’s assessment of Taylor as a visionary.

One former employee, who asked not to be named, said the committed runner didn’t have much to choose from before Tracksmith, describing the industry’s 2014 offerings as “neon, boring, and not high performance.” Tracksmith took the better products the pros were getting and gave them to amateurs. (And though the price point was initially surprising, these days, in the era of $300 super shoes, it seems reasonable.)

But getting eyeballs on a new business is cash intensive, and Taylor had big, expensive operations, which included stipends for unsponsored Olympic Marathon Trials qualifiers and hosting twilight 5Ks for the fast amateurs looking to run PRs. Real estate on Newbury Street and in Brooklyn does not come cheap, either. A London location that opened in 2023 closed in August.

Without Taylor, does the brand have legs? The fear is that it becomes “performance J.Crew,” preppy running apparel without the investment in the sport.

In response to a question about bolstering the sport, the Tracksmith spokesperson confirmed the company would be continuing with its programming and support of amateur runners through clubs and meets like Tracksmith Stamata, the Twilight series, Hare AC, and the Amateur Support Program. “Nothing has changed or will change there,” the spokesperson said.

But with Taylor’s departure, some see Tracksmith being at a crossroads, caught between funders seeking a return on their investment and fast-growing competition.

“I think a lot of investors, private equity investors, they revere founders and understand that the business that they’re in, particularly one like this, it’s as much of a cultural business as anything else,” said Ryan Eckel, who worked for Tracksmith as the brand president for five years, from 2019 to 2024. “And when you start treating it like it’s making widgets, I think you lose sight [of the culture] and ultimately I think it hurts their investments long term.”

Powell, though, still sees a lane for Tracksmith, especially with consumers who are willing to pay premium prices.

“On one level, I would tell you there's never been a better time to be a small brand, because I think the consumer is looking for unique products,” he said. “But because the consumer is always demanding new and next, that part is really hard for a small brand to execute.”

Sarah Lorge Butler is a writer and editor living in Eugene, Oregon, and her stories about the sport, its trends, and fascinating individuals have appeared in Runner’s World since 2005. She is the author of two popular fitness books, Run Your Butt Off! and Walk Your Butt Off!

#8963. How Triathlon and Incurable Cancer Have Given Me a Way to Live Despite My Diagnosis

Age-group triathlete Rebecca Jaussi shares her personal story with Triathlete of how receiving a cancer diagnosis drove her to signing up for and racing an Ironman 70.3.

I have spent most of my life making plans.

Endless lists of goals. Race calendars. Career milestones. Bucket-list adventures. I have always believed that if I worked hard enough and planned carefully enough, I might chart the course of my life.

Running and occasional triathlons are at the top of my goal-making lists.

I was a late starter professionally, choosing to stay home with my children when they were young. When I eventually returned to school, I didn’t ease my way back in. I was accepted into an accelerated doctoral nursing program, completing an intense year of coursework and clinicals before becoming a registered nurse, followed by three years of doctoral study. In 2020, I earned my doctorate in nursing practice and became a family nurse practitioner.

I have always been willing to push myself, physically and mentally, and my tenacity has benefited me.

I never imagined I would need it to fight cancer.

This story began with a fall. It was another beautiful morning on the North Shore of Oahu (where I was living at the time) in February 2023, and I was running a technical trail when I went down on a rocky section. I experienced a pop in my right hamstring and some pain. But I did what I always do and just kept going.

I finished the run. I experienced some pain afterward, but not enough, in my mind, to stop running for good. I took a few days off and then returned to the trails.

As a healthcare provider, I knew better. But as a runner, I convinced myself otherwise.

I continued running through an increasingly persistent, insidious pain. Eventually, my pace deteriorated from slow to a limping shuffle. Finally, I went to my colleague who practiced sports medicine, and was referred to physical therapy.

I started PT in May. My physical therapist told me I needed to stop running, and I thought that was an unreasonable course of action. There have been very few occasions in my life when I stopped running, including childbirth and surgery, and they were brief periods of time.

Running wasn’t simply exercise for me; it was where I found my flow state and truly part of my identity.

I didn’t feel ready or willing to give up running due to the pain but trusted my physical therapist, whom I considered a friend and a respected colleague, that this was the best course of action.

For three months, I walked on flat trails. I continued my physical therapy exercises and cross-trained but abstained from running or hiking.

When I returned for another assessment, my physical therapist was puzzled. I wasn’t improving. He suggested imaging, and that push changed everything.

I went in for an MRI of my right leg. The imaging was ordered for my mid-thigh, which was not where I had originally injured my hamstring. When I discussed this with the technician, I pointed out that it was in my hip region, so he modified the imaging order.

The MRI showed enlarged lymph nodes in my right groin, hip, and possibly behind my knee, which was an abnormal finding.

I had no recent infection or other obvious explanation for the swollen lymph nodes. I asked colleagues and peers for their opinions, and most believed this was a benign finding.

My mind vacillated between thinking that it was probably fine and the worst-case scenario of malignancy. It felt unsettling to me, and I decided to push for a biopsy rather than wait a few months for an ultrasound to see if the lymph nodes were still enlarged.

After the biopsy, I waited eight grueling days for the results. The physician, who was also my colleague and friend, told me the findings indicated that I had a form of B-cell non-Hodgkin lymphoma.

This was not easy to ingest, but I didn’t want to burden her with the heaviness of this diagnosis and began joking around. I was blasé and asked her, “How are we going to fix my leg so that I can run?” refusing to fall apart on the phone.

Then I hung up and broke down in front of my husband. Suddenly, all the plans I had spent my life making seemed irrelevant. Questions revolved in my head. What would happen to my family? My future? My career?

The next step I took was to do what I knew how to do, which was research my diagnosis to find out everything that I could about it. I wanted to know the prognosis, treatment options, statistics, anything to help me wrap my head around this.

What I discovered in this process was much more difficult to accept. There were things that I could not control.

I was driven to face the possibility that I may not live as long as I had expected. I had to accept that I would be living with the uncertainty of my health status and that fighting incurable cancer might become a permanent fixture in my life.

For someone who had devoted decades to building goals and marking off boxes, this was terrifying. There were no checklists for this.

I took time to process what I was facing and came to the recognition that I had a choice – not about living with cancer, but about living my life.

I was not going to allow this diagnosis to define me; I had a strong desire to live my life to the fullest with purpose and direction. I still wanted to work as a nurse practitioner for as long as I could. I still wanted to pursue medical humanitarian work. I still wanted to travel. I still wanted to be active.

In January, I was accepted into a clinical trial for immunotherapy.

Before treatment began, I did something that probably sounded slightly unreasonable to the people around me.

I signed up for Ironman 70.3 Hawaii on June 1, 2024.

I asked my oncologist and the lead investigator of my clinical trial whether I could participate. They told me that I was the first patient they knew of to ask about competing in a half Ironman while undergoing treatment.

They gave me their blessing with one caveat: It would be essential to listen to my body. This was going to be physically taxing on my body due to the cancer already exhausting my body and undergoing treatment in addition to the rigors of training for a 70.3.

I understood the risks. I also understood something else: Training gave me a goal and purpose to keep moving.

Although cancer had taken away my perception of control, it hadn’t taken away my ability to choose a direction.

I arrived in Kona on May 30, 2024. I was nervous and exhausted. I had received treatment the week before and was still recovering from it.

My younger brother, who had agreed to race with me when I asked, and I gathered our swag and attended the informational session. As we were walking out, I saw the iconic walls of all the participants, their bib numbers, and the “why” wall. Seeing my “why” story on the wall solidified my resolve in what I was doing.

The day before the race, I started receiving text messages with their pictures attached, early in the morning, from friends, family, and my whole care team from Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center, wearing a T-shirt that had my cancer ribbon with the words “Fight Cancer Like a Girl” on the front and “Team Rebecca 01” on the back. My amazing husband made nearly 100 shirts and sent them out, asking them to send me a picture and words of encouragement the day before the race. I felt so much love and support from the people in my life.

On June 1, 2024, I stood on the beach waiting for my wave to start at Ironman 70.3 Hawaii. I remember feeling incredibly grateful to be there and have the ability to push my body to the limits.

The race was hard; the winds were cranking so hard that several cyclists were blown into the lava rocks along the highway. It took some serious grit to keep going, but with my husband and kids driving by with my favorite songs blasting on the stereo, cheering me on, I was able to finish the bike.

By the time I started the run, it was midday, and the sun was searing, with temperatures climbing above 90 degrees. My body was fatigued, and every part of me wanted the race to be done. I dug deep. My mantra was “I can do hard things” on repeat. I kept moving.

During those final miles, rolling thoughts in my head surfaced: If I can fight cancer, I can finish this race.

There was an alteration in my thinking and in the purpose of that day; this was no longer about the race but rather an understanding that I was capable of moving forward.

I crossed the finish line with my brother beside me and my family waiting and cheering. I was overwhelmed by my emotions as I crossed the line.

My body was spent; however, there was something strangely beautiful about that exhaustion. I would rather be exhausted from swimming, cycling, and running than exhausted from lying still, consumed by the knowledge that I have incurable cancer.

My training looks different than it used to. Some days are hard, and my body needs downtime.

I’ve learned that listening to my body isn’t a weakness, or even optional at times, but rather a way for me to keep up the fight.

With every step I take, every mile I cycle, every lap that I swim, it is more than just training; it serves as a reminder that my body is still mine and truly a gift to be cherished.

My cancer diagnosis has altered my relationship with time. I functioned at a faster pace and was always thinking ahead about what was next: the next race, the next degree, the next goal, the next item to add to my list.

I am more focused on the mile that I am in right now. I have not stopped making plans; I just hold them differently.

My desires to work, travel, race, and serve others remain, but their priority and intensity are more flexible, as my health and energy can be fluid.

This diagnosis has shifted my perspective – I no longer believe that my worth or value depends on completing every goal I write down.

Some days a win is simply to get out the door. Sometimes it is a slow swim, and the distance may be shorter than planned. Sometimes it is walking instead of running. Sometimes it is resting.

And sometimes, it is standing at a finish line I wasn’t sure I would ever reach.

The trajectory of my life feels unsure and more constrained. However, I know that running, swimming, and cycling are things I can do at the moment, and they make me feel alive.

Honestly, for me, that’s what endurance sport has become. This is not a means of escape from cancer but rather my way of living despite it.

One step, one mile, one breath, I will keep going.
