#8949. 12 Road Bikes Our Editors Would Actually Buy, From $1,200 All-Rounders to Dream-Bike Builds

From budget aluminum builds to pro-level carbon machines, these road bikes are worth buying.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Over the past year, I’ve spent more time on road bikes than any other type. Why? Because, like for many cyclists, taking a road ride is easier than getting out on a gravel or mountain bike. For road rides, you don’t need to drive to the trailhead or the champagne gravel; simply change into your cycling clothes, grab a helmet, and start riding. This makes road rides great for time-crunched workouts or for a quick mental reset.

Today’s road bikes offer many advantages over those from only a decade ago. Aerodynamic frame designs make many road bikes stand out visually; they also help you ride faster and pedal longer distances with less effort. Wide tires (sometimes up to 35mm) and disc brakes (often hydraulic) provide more comfort, better control, and all-weather performance than the skinny rubber and rim brakes of older road models. Many road bikes also feature electronic shifting that changes gears faster, smoother, and with less effort than cable-actuated shifting, and electronic systems typically require less maintenance.

However, road bikes aren’t only for racing, flat-out speed, or fitness; many of the best road bikes prioritize rider comfort and safety. Other great road bikes incorporate features that make them versatile enough for commuting or multi-day trips. Bicycle companies offer several varieties of road bikes designed to meet the riding demands, bike fit needs, budgets, and personal style of almost any rider. Dozens of brands make road bikes for every type of cyclist: from new riders to elite racers, and everyone in between.

We consider most bicycles with slick (or mostly slick) tires, intended for riding on paved (or mostly paved) surfaces, as “road bikes.” These bikes are usually equipped with dropbars, 700c wheels, and narrow tires. You will find two main styles of bikes in the road category. While bicycle brands give categories fancy marketing names, the two groups are best described as “race bikes” and “ride bikes.”

➡️ Race bikes prioritize speed and performance, often with a more aggressive riding position and a stiff feel. Sub-groups of race bikes include aerobikes and lightweight bikes.

➡️ Ride bikes (often labeled “endurance bikes”) can still be ridden fast and are often as light as race bikes. Ride bikes typically use a more upright riding position, and wider tires enhance comfort and control.

Senior Test Editor Matt Phillip’s story, “Why Race Bikes Aren’t Real Road Bikes,” discusses this distinction and why we think race bikes aren’t the best choice for most road riders.

Gravel bikes are another popular dropbar bike option, and they share characteristics with road bikes. However, their knobbier tires and frame geometry make them better suited to unpaved surfaces and even some mountain bike trails than riding on blacktop. Read our Gravel Bike Guide for more details on this bike type.

Specialized’s Aethos goes against dominant road cycling trends. Most road bikes feature aerodynamic tube shapes and deep-profile wheels to reduce watts and improve speed, but these details often add weight and negatively impact ride quality. On the Aethos, Specialized concentrated on low weight and excellent road feel—and we love the results. In his review of the second-generation Aethos, Matt Phillips sums up the ride feel: “I’d say it feels like a hyper light, stiff carbon bike, but the feedback is like that of a beautifully tuned steel bike. Which is kind of ideal, really.”

For the Aethos 2, Specialized adds a UDH dropout and a more upright riding position. Plus, the frame and fork now clear tires up to 35mm wide. These updates give the Aethos 2 amazing versatility and add comfort for long days in the saddle. Best of all, the Aethos 2 Expert model (with SRAM Force AXS components) weighs only 15.9 pounds.

The Synapse is Cannondale’s endurance road line. Designed for comfort and versatility, these models feature shorter reach and a more upright riding position than Cannondale’s race bikes. The Synapse 2 combines the line’s core features into a budget-friendly package; it’s a great option for fitness, commuting, or light touring.

The Synapse’s aluminum frame—available in seven sizes from 44cm to 61cm—includes eyelets for adding racks, fenders, and bags. Plus, it fits tires up to 32mm wide. The Synapse 2 comes with tubeless-ready wheels and a Shimano Cues 10-speed drivetrain. Paired with 46/32-tooth chainrings and an 11–39T cassette, the gear range is wider than many road bikes, highlighted by a super-low gear for climbing hills or when loaded up with bags for commutes or bikepacking.

While Cannondale doesn’t equip the Synapse 2 with its innovative SmartSense system (found on higher-priced Synapse Carbon bikes), you can add it later using a downtube adapter to power integrated front and rear lights and rear-facing radar.

When shopping for a road bike, it can be tough to find a decent-quality bike at a good price. Many high-priced bikes are over-equipped for riders. However, low-cost bikes often use off-brand parts, rim brakes, and quick-release wheels.

For $1,200, the Van Rysel EDR 2 AF is a solid bike for the money. It has a double-butted aluminum frame (it fits racks and fenders), a carbon fork, thru axle wheels, and disc brakes. Van Rysel uses industry-standard component sizing (instead of proprietary parts), so you have more options for compatible parts as you wear out components or want to make upgrades.

The launch of X-Lab in the U.S. is one of the year’s biggest cycling stories, and the brand’s exceptionally-priced bikes have created a huge buzz among riders, bike shops, and media. This attention is warranted: the X-Lab models we’ve ridden have performed great—especially for the price.

X-Lab is an offshoot of XDS, a large China-based bicycle company. XDS sells its own models in many regions; it’s also one of the world’s largest bike and frame manufacturers, with a long history producing OEM high-end carbon frames and forks for many brands—including bicycles you may have ridden, seen raced in the Tour, or lusted after. That manufacturing and engineering expertise, along with massive buying power, enables X-Lab to offer its bikes for thousands of dollars less than bikes from almost any other brand.

A great example of this is X-Lab’s AD8. For $4,500, you get: a WorldTour-proven aero frameset, full carbon wheels (even the spokes!), a carbon crank with power meter, a one-piece carbon cockpit, and a Shimano 105 Di2 groupset. The AD8 even has a carbon-railed Selle Italia saddle.

The lowest price in the world wouldn’t matter if the AD8 didn’t ride well. Luckily, it does. The bike’s geometry and road feel are similar to the Canyon Aeroad, another excellent road race bike. In his full review of the AD8, Test Editor Dan Chabanov said, “It looks fast, and it even makes the woosh-woosh sound of going fast. Everything about it screams speed from the moment you get on it. It has the stiffness and jump that a top-end race bike should have.”

Scott’s Addict RC blends lightweight with aggressive geometry that feels better the harder you push yourself and the bike. It’s one of the rare road race bikes that is as confident on fast, twisty descents as on double-digit gradient climbs. And at a little over 17 pounds for the Shimano 105 Di2-equipped RC 30 model, its weight competes with many far pricier road bikes.

The Addict RC’s geometry gives the bike its descending prowess. The bike is low and long—more BB drop, a longer reach, and a lower stack than the previous-gen Addict. The bike is lower and longer than most competitors in the category, so it’s not ideal for riders who need an upright position or like a mellow-riding road machine. But for those who like a spicy ride, it’s an extremely fun road bike.

The words “Pinarello” and “value” don’t typically fit together. However, the legendary Italian brand provides a solid package at a reasonable price with its X1 model.

As Matt Phillips explained in his review of the F7 road racing model, Pinarello’s road bikes are renowned for precise handling and excellent ride feel—as well as high prices and aggressive race-bike fit geometry. Pinarello flipped that script on the X1, delivering an endurance bike for less than a quarter of the price tag of its top-tier models.

Pinarello achieves this price by using some lower-grade carbon fiber and cost-saving component choices. Fortunately, the X1 doesn’t compromise on shifting and braking performance or bike fit. Pinarello equips the X1 with Shimano’s superb 105 12-speed mechanical-shifting groupset and offers an impressive nine frame sizes. However, the bike’s Shimano WH-RS171 wheelset begs for an upgrade to match the frameset’s potential.

When you’re new to road riding, picking the right bike can be challenging since you might not know exactly what type of road rides you’ll enjoy. That’s why bikes with a balanced approach and a good price—like the Specialized Allez—are the perfect choice for new cyclists. And they’re also great for experienced riders looking for a solid bike at a reasonable price.

The Allez provides a snappier ride that transmits the feel of the road in a palpable, yet not overbearing way. It fits wide tires (up to 35mm), and Specialized equips the Allez with Shimano Cues 10-speed components, which feature a wide gear range and sure-stopping hydraulic disc brakes.

The Allez’s ride feel won’t be confused with its carbon cousins like the Aethos 2 or Tarmac SL, and its handling isn’t as razor-sharp as the Allez Sprint aluminum race bike. However, the Allez is a well-rounded, capable road bike at a great price; it’s sure to please many cyclists.

Trek’s Domane was one of the first dedicated endurance road bikes when it was launched 14 years ago. The recently released fifth-generation platform adds versatility while stripping weight. It did this by removing IsoSpeed from the Domane, a decoupler system which provided vertical compliance over rough terrain, and was the platform’s signature feature.

Instead of building a system into the frame, Trek replaced IsoSpeed with plump, 35mm-wide tires. It’s a simple change that absorbs road chatter and soaks up potholes without adding weight, cost, or maintenance complexities. Wide tires also improve control and traction on less-than-perfect road surfaces.

Trek offers ten Domane models, priced from $2,400 to $15,000. The second bike in the lineup, the Domane SL 5 $2,700 gives you 35mm tubeless tires, a 2x12 Shimano 105 mechanical shifting drivetrain, and hydraulic disc brakes. It’s a solid all-road bike that handles everything from training to commuting, and even some dirt road adventures.

In his review of Canyon’s Endurace AllRoad for Bicycling’s 2026 Bike Awards, Matt Phillips wrote, “There are cheap bikes that are pretty good for the money, and then there’s the Canyon Endurace Allroad, which is the more irritating kind of value because it makes you wonder what excuse everybody else has. At $1,499, this bike has no business feeling this complete.”

The Endurace AllRoad checks all the right boxes for a solid endurance road bike: aluminum frame, carbon fork, 40mm tire clearance, Shimano Cues 2x10, hydraulic disc brakes, and useful bag mounts. The bike provides a quiet, smooth, and calm ride on the road. When the pavement gets rough, Phillips says it is “quick enough to stay lively, stable enough to feel composed”.

Overall, the Endurace AllRoad is a low-priced endurance bike that rides like models costing twice its $1,500 price.

Many road riders love race bikes for their low weight and lively feel, even if they never pin up a number and compete. Cannondale recently launched its fifth-generation SuperSix Evo road race bike. While the new Evo looks similar to its predecessor, it includes several upgrades and refinements that push it to the top of the Best Race Bikes of 2026.

The biggest change for the Gen-5 SuperSix Evo is its refined geometry. Cannondale lowered the stack height by 10mm. This helps riders achieve a lower handlebar height and a roomier cockpit feel. The brand also added a frame size (separate 50cm and 52cm sizes instead of a 51cm), which should help more riders achieve their needed bike fit. Cannondale offers several SuperSix Evo models, ranging from the $5,000 Evo 5 to the 13.8-pound Evo Lab71 SL at $13,500.

While they weigh more than carbon models, titanium bikes have excellent ride feel, great durability, and classic looks. Unfortunately, titanium costs a lot, and it’s tricky to weld. Combined, that typically makes titanium frames cost significantly more than equivalent carbon or steel bikes. However, small Truckee, California-based brand BlackHeart offers amazing-riding titanium (and aluminum, too) bikes at very competitive prices.

As I said in the opening paragraph of my review of the bike, “The BlackHeart Road Plus Ti is the type of bike most dropbar riders actually need. It’s fast and nimble like a good road bike, while also accommodating generously wide tires. Plus, it’s reasonably lightweight, rides incredibly smoothly, and has solid geometry.”

BlackHeart sells the Road Plus Ti as a frameset for $3,499 or built up with SRAM AXS XPLR groupsets starting at $5,799 (for Rival). A bonus of buying from BlackHeart is the brand’s great service and customization; you can change component sizing, pick your tires, upgrade the wheels, or add a power meter to your bike. BlackHeart will even custom-paint your fork practically any color for a $300 upcharge.

The Cervélo Soloist was one of the first aerobikes in the pro peloton and helped bring wind-slicing technology to road bikes. Now known as the S-series, the Cervélo-sponsored Visma-Lease a Bike Pro team has won some of the world’s most prestigious races on this frame.

True to its heritage, the S5 is a professional-level aerobike designed for those who love to go fast. Cervélo’s engineers optimized every shape on this bike so it zips through the air with minimal resistance; you feel the S5’s speed from your first pedal strokes. While the bike is brilliantly quick, it’s also extremely stiff and responsive, so the S5 isn’t your best bet if you value comfort over speed.

The S5 won’t turn you into Jonas, Wout, Marianne, or Sepp, but it does help you have fun trying.

The bikes in this story range from excellent $1,200 all-arounders to high-performance, dream machines priced well over $10,000—and they’re all great bikes. This is what you can expect to get for your money in 2026.

Road bikes priced under $1,200 typically come with rim or mechanical disc brakes and 8- or 9-speed drivetrains. These are great for flat or rolling terrain, but may feel sluggish on long or steep climbs due to their heavier weight and narrower gear range.

Bikes costing $1,200 to $2,000 typically come with aluminum frames, disc brakes, and 9- to 10-speed drivetrains. Many bikes at this price now come with hydraulic disc brakes, which offer improved stopping power with reduced maintenance compared to rim or cable-actuated disc brakes.

When spending $2,000 to $4,000, you often get a bike that looks and rides like a premium road bike, only heavier. These bikes usually come equipped with 11- or 12-speed drivetrains, disc brakes, and a carbon fork. Some models in this price range feature carbon frames.

In the $4,000 to $6,000 range, expect carbon frames and forks, high-end components, and higher-quality finishing. These bikes also offer significant weight savings over lower-cost road bikes. Electronic shifting, upgraded wheels, and carbon handlebars, stems, and seatposts are common, making these bikes feel faster and more responsive.

Above $6,000, you're paying for top-tier craftsmanship, premium materials, and high-performance parts. Road bikes at this price often feature the same frames as bikes ridden by pros in races like the Tour de France.

Finally, don’t forget to account for accessories and gear when budgeting for a road bike purchase. Remember to factor in items like a helmet, shoes, pedals, bottles, and riding clothes into your total price.

#8948. Magnus Ditlev Sets New Iron-Distance World Best With 7:19:17 at Ironman Florida

Magnus Ditlev of Denmark wins the 2026 IRONMAN Florida in a World Record Time of 7:19:17 on November 7, 2026 in Panama City, Florida. (Photo by Donald Miralle/Getty Images for IRONMAN) (Photo: Getty Images for IRONMAN)

One month after a heartbreaking DNF in Kona, Magnus Ditlev (DEN) rode away from the field at Ironman Florida and never looked back. His 7:19:17 took 1:47 off the previous men’s iron-distance world best that Sam Laidlow (FRA) set at Challenge Roth earlier this year.

Florida was a chance at redemption for Ditlev, who had come agonizingly close to winning the Ironman World Championship in Kona. He’d taken the lead late on the bike and looked on course for the win until he abruptly came to a stop on the run with roughly 30 minutes of racing left.

However, ahead of Kona, Ditlev said he was putting up career-best numbers across the swim, bike, and run at his training camp in Colorado. In Florida, he finally got to reap the rewards of what fitness could produce all the way to the finish line.

Ditlev came out of the water in fifth, right on the heels of Ben Kanute (USA) and Rudy von Berg (USA). He took his time in T1 and started the bike nearly a minute down, but it didn’t take him long to ride back to the front. And then, just past mile 10, he made his move. No one could go with him, and they wouldn’t be able to stay remotely close to him either.

By the time Ditlev came off the bike, he was 11 minutes clear of a chase group that included Sam Long (USA), von Berg, and Kanute. His 3:51:16 was the fastest bike split ever recorded at an Ironman, nearly two minutes quicker than the 3:53:12 Robert Kallin (SWE) rode at Ironman Kalmar in August.

Off the bike, he once again took his time in transition. But transitions were the only slow part of Ditlev’s day. Once through T2, he picked up another minute on the chasers over the opening 10 miles. He hit halfway in 1:15, on pace for a 2:30 marathon and well within reach of Laidlow’s 7:21:04. With such an unassailable lead, one can assume he must’ve known the record was within reach to keep such an aggressive pace.

Ditlev eventually closed with a 2:33:31 marathon, crossing the line in 7:19:17. Von Berg took second, 14 minutes back, securing the early Kona slot and podium he’d come for. Matt Hanson (USA), meanwhile, ran a remarkable 2:28:07 to beat Long to the final podium spot, but still finished 16 minutes behind Ditlev.

#8947. The 6 Best Walking Pads for Staying Active During the Workday

Improve your focus and get your steps in seamlessly with one of these walking pads.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

Stuck at your desk all day? Us, too—and we work for a running publication. (Oh, the irony!) Well, fret not, fellow office warriors: Walking pads and under-desk treadmills are here to save the day—and boost your step count. These low-profile treadmills slide right under your standing desk, making it easy to walk and work at the same time. Thanks to a renewed focus on health, whether you’re working from home or heading into the office, walking pads have quickly become a staple in home offices and shared workspaces alike. So, whether you’re aiming to close those rings or boost your daily steps, a walking pad can help you stay active throughout the workday without missing that 3 p.m. meeting.

🏃🏻‍♀️ Ready to unlock a stronger, healthier you? Our Walking for Weight Loss Guide can make it happen!

Recent studies support the benefits of movement while working: office employees using treadmill desks have reported improved energy, greater focus, and a boosted mood over just a few months of consistent use. Plus, the convenience of walking pads means you can exercise regardless of the weather or your schedule—no gym membership required. With so many walking pads on the market, each offering a unique blend of features and portability, at a range of prices, finding the right model can be overwhelming. Not to worry, though. We put tens of thousands of steps on these machines to find the best ones for you.

If you’re looking for portability, a cushioned deck, affordability, and a walking pad you can use while you’re in the office without people on your meeting hearing your treadmill? This is the one for you. We’ve had it at HQ for years, and it’s consistently in use by our team. It has seen thousands of miles, and it’s still going.

It’s got a well-cushioned deck that absorbs impact, a motor built for heavier walkers, and it’s relatively wide for a walking pad. It is, however, a bit short front-to-back, but it’s fine for most people. If you’re a giant like my brother? You might want a different model, otherwise, this is just about perfect.

If your social feeds are overflowing with DeerRun under-desk walking pads, you’re not alone. This TikTok-famous gadget is everywhere, and for good reason: It’s a simple, space-saving treadmill that you can control with a remote or an app.

The app’s got your back, letting you dial up the speed without breaking a sweat (or your focus). And topping out at just over 3 mph, it’s more of a gentle stroll than a full-on sprint.

The deck’s a cozy—if kinda tight—35 by 16 inches, which means it’ll tuck neatly under your desk. It’s easy to use and that glorious cushioned feel is pure bliss for your feet while you’re getting those steps in.

This is our office’s new BFF. The most frequent user, Hype Director Aly Ellis, said that her favorite feature is the convenience, noting “I prefer this one to one with arms because it allows me to adjust the desk height when I need to for comfort purposes.” She’s also a big fan of the fact that it lights up, but mostly because it’s cool. I agree. She does worry about losing the remote, as we all do, but fun fact! You can operate it via the app, so there’s no real worry there.

It’s quiet and sturdy, has a 12 percent incline, and has a high weight limit, so larger-bodied walkers should feel comfortable on this walking pad.

This is easily the most compact on this list. It folds up to about the size of a queen blanket, but it doesn’t feel flimsy or cheap. WalkingPad has made it its business to build high-quality walking pads that are made for your home or office.

I like this one because it’s no fuss, no muss, has a large 48-inch by 16-inch walking surface, weighs only 50 pounds, and it’s whisper quiet.

The Urevo Strol 2.0 walking pad is the under-desk treadmill you want if you tend toward boredom. It has a ton of built-in programming, and the ability to connect to a ton more like Zwift.

Once you link the app to your phone, you can control everything right there. But, if that’s not your style, traditional controls are easy to access and use. It’s a smooth walk, quieter than previous models, and you can move it around easily.

The combination of the sturdy tablet holder and smart app integration creates a user-friendly experience that blends exercise with productivity or entertainment effortlessly in any space.

If you’ve ever wondered how hard you can push yourself while you work, do I have the walking pad for you. This puppy inclines all the way to 14 percent, which—whoa—and it does it with the power of a brushless motor, which makes it quieter (though it can’t quiet your huffing and puffing), and that same motor will last a lot longer than others thanks to its construction.

The whole thing is remote controlled, so when you’re fighting for your life and you don’t want your Teams meeting to see it, you can quickly adjust on the fly.

When shopping for the best under-desk walking pad, keep these factors in mind:

Size and Portability: Ensure the walking pad’s dimensions fit under your desk and in your workspace. Consider weight and whether the machine has wheels for easy storage or movement.

Belt Size: Wider belts provide more stability and comfort, while narrower pads are better for tight spaces. Longer deck lengths work best for those with a longer stride.

Speed Range: Most walking pads offer speeds from 0.5 to 4 mph—enough for gentle walking to brisk paces. Some 2-in-1 pads allow faster speeds when used away from a desk.

Incline Options: A few models feature adjustable inclines for varied intensity, though many are flat for multitasking. If you want more of a workout, look for pads with at least a minor incline capability.

Weight Capacity: Check each machine’s weight limit, especially if you need extra support or want a more robust frame.

Noise Level: Choose a quiet pad for minimal distraction, particularly if you share your space with others or take calls frequently.

Ease of Use: Look for simple controls (often via remote) and clear displays. Consider features like app compatibility, folding capabilities, and maintenance requirements.

Price: Budget models are available for under $200, while high-end or commercial-grade options cost significantly more. Decide which features are worth extra investment for your specific needs.

So, what’s the difference between a treadmill and a walking pad? There are a lot of parallels for sure, and functionally they’re very similar. However, the real difference between a treadmill and a walking pad happens under the hood. Walking pads have smaller, quieter motors that don’t allow you to pick up the pace dramatically, but they keep them quiet enough to use while you work or read. They’re also a lot lower to the ground, and that low step height makes them a great choice for folks who have joint and mobility issues. They’re shorter and narrower than traditional treadmills so that they fit easily under desks. Luckily, they’re also easier to store, and many of them fold into little packages or can be stored on their side. And the point many people love the most? They’re usually a lot cheaper.

Our team performed all walking pad testing either in our offices for hundreds of hours or in our own homes, reflecting the real-world environments where these products are most used. Each unit was assessed with a focus on:

Speed and Incline: We measured each pad’s speed range and, where available, incline adjustments, making sure transitions were smooth and controls responsive.

Noise: We operated pads during conference calls and regular work to evaluate how quietly each model ran.

Design and Portability: We checked for ease of setup, the ability to move and store the pad, and whether the design fit under multiple desk types.

User Experience: Testers of varying heights and stride lengths used each pad for sessions extending beyond an hour, noting comfort, usability, and any unique features or challenges.

Every product featured here was rigorously tested for durability, performance, and portability in the Runner’s World offices and in the homes of our editors, ensuring our recommendations are both practical and trustworthy. Whether you’re a remote worker, student, or just trying to reduce your sedentary hours, our comprehensive guide will help you find the best under-desk walking pad to fit your space and support your movement goals.

#8946. The Time of Day You Exercise Could Help Control Blood Sugar

Any physical activity is good for your metabolic health, but research says timing it right may have more benefits for your glucose levels.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Although blood sugar control is essential for those with diabetes, it’s also key for maintaining health overall. Research indicates that blood sugar levels can affect a range of physical functions, including hormone regulation, body composition, digestive processes, and even cognitive health.

That’s why keeping control of blood glucose levels is important, and one way to help might include doing moderate- to vigorous-intensity exercise in the evening, according to a study publish in Obesity.

Researchers looked at 186 men and women who were overweight or had obesity and were diagnosed with at least one metabolic impairment, such as high blood pressure or high cholesterol. Over a 14-day period, researchers tracked their physical activity and glucose levels, along with the time of day for exercise. Morning exercise was defined as before noon, with afternoon exercise between noon and 6:00 p.m, and evening exercise after that.

At the end of the two weeks, those who did more than 50 percent of their exercise in the evening had significantly lower glucose levels compared to those who were sedentary, and better glucose regulation than participants who mainly exercised in the mornings or afternoons.

The effects were especially notable for those who’d struggled with regulating their blood sugar before participating in the study, according to co-author Antonia Clavero Jimeno, Ph.D.(c), researcher in the department of physical education and sports at the University of Granada in Spain.

Although the study participants were specifically chosen based on metabolic factors and sedentary behavior, he told Bicycling that previous evidence has shown that the results might be the same for those without those factors, and who already exercise regularly.

“In fact, the impact of both physical activity volume and timing for glycemic control may be amplified in those with higher activity levels,” he said.

That’s backed up by previous research looking at active people who were assessed for blood sugar changes based on when they exercised. In that study, published in 2022, those who performed moderate-to-vigorous activity in the afternoon had 18 percent lower insulin resistance compared to morning exercisers, and the evening group fared even better, with a 25 percent reduction in insulin resistance.

One factor that was not explored in either study was the role of dietary changes, and this is an area that needs more research, said Clavero Jimeno. Determining whether a strategy like time-restricted eating—also called intermittent fasting—would be helpful or harmful to glucose regulation when paired with evening exercise is a next step, and is already being studied by Clavero Jimeno and his team. (Some research published this year suggests intermittent fasting may have promising effects on blood sugar regulation, at least in those with type 2 diabetes.)

“Dietary intake is, of course, recognized as crucial for glycemic control, and may influence the results overall,” Clavero Jimeno said. “But in the absence of that information, this current study does emphasize that if you want better control of your glucose levels, evening exercise, done at a higher intensity, may be beneficial.”

#8944. This Seated Twist Stretches Your Spine, Engages Your Core, and Enhances Your Awareness

If you buy through our links, we may earn an affiliate commission. This supports our mission to get more people active and outside.Learn about Outside Online's affiliate link policy

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about a seated twist first appeared in the March-April 1994 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

To encourage new perceptual skills in my students, I like to ask them from time to time to practice in a new spot in the yoga studio. If you’re like most people, after a few classes you find yourself regularly gravitating to the same location, often within a few inches of accuracy.

The mere suggestion to place your mat in the front of the room instead of the cozy corner may make you decidedly un-comfortable. Changing positions enables you to see yourself and the world from a different vantage point, much as a photographer might circle a subject to get pictures from different angles.

It’s not surprising, considering the propensity of our species to form habits, that we tend to perceive our bodies from one perspective, including some aspects of ourselves while leaving others out.

Thus our perception of our body may become like a two-dimensional sketch, deprived of the volume, form, and texture that would extend our awareness into the three-dimensional realm. While Eastern cultures have investigated and honored the inner layers of the body as the key to our physical, mental, and spiritual health, most Western cultures have concerned themselves primarily with the body’s superficial layers. Because of this bias, most of us have come to view our movements as entirely dictated by the muscles and bones, unconsciously deleting other systems from our awareness. Keeping the mind on the outer layers, we become unable to feel or act from our deeper selves.

One of the body systems that brings us most succinctly into a deeper sense of self are the organs, the contents of the musculoskeletal container. Awareness of the organs gives our movements volume, form, and a sense of ripe fullness. Through the health and vitality of the organs, the outer layers gain their strength and form.

Just as we might bring our attention to the sensation of a muscle stretching, we can bring our attention to the sensation of an internal organ. When we change the vantage point of our awareness to bring the inner body into the foreground (an inner adjustment analogous to moving to a different place in the yoga studio), the way we experience ourselves and the quality of our movement will be quite different.

For most of recorded history, yogis have been engaged in just this kind of research, exploring the effects that the asanas (as well as pranayama and meditation) have on the deeper, subtler bodily systems. The ancient practitioners noted which movements and practices stimulated, purified, sedated, or neutralized the energy currents moving deep within the body, correlating these phenomena to health, longevity, and the elevation of consciousness. By contrast, they were not terribly interested in the state of their hamstring muscles, and traditional texts make few references to such structures.

Movements that twist the body compress, elongate, and massage the inner organs. Unfortunately, twists are often practiced exclusively from the perspective of the musculoskeletal system; we use the strength of the muscles and the leverage of the bones to force the body into rotation without ever inviting the soft inner contents along for the ride. Focusing on the internal organs not only reduces the possibility of injury, but stimulates and tones these deep structures by bringing our attention to them, just as electrical activity is created in our muscles simply by visualizing them flexing.

In this article, we’re going to look at how changing the vantage point of our awareness affects the practice of Pose Dedicated to the Sage Marichi (Marichyasana III), a seated twist.

Bringing attention to the inner body is a way to physically organize our presence on this center. Knowing that there is nowhere to “get to,” we can proceed with the full knowledge that we are on our way.

The following exercise was adapted from Sensing, Feeling, and Action by Bonnie Bainbridge Cohen. Sit on a cushion or blanket with your legs crossed. Close your eyes and let yourself settle. Bring your awareness to the soft inner contents of the torso surrounded by the musculoskeletal container. Imagine your body as two concentric cylinders with the soft internal organs on the inside and the harder musculoskeletal system surrounding them. Feel how the rise and fall of the breath swells from the core and communicates itself to the outer layer.

Now gently bring your awareness to each of your major organs. In the chest is the heart, slightly to the left of center, with the lungs on either side. In the upper left quadrant of the abdomen is the stomach; in the upper right quadrant of the belly is the liver, which extends up underneath the rib cage. The small intestines occupy most of the central and lower belly. In the lower right quadrant of the belly, the small intestine becomes the large intestine, which makes a hairpin turn to run up the right side of the belly (the ascending colon), across the top (the transverse colon), and down the left side (the descending colon), finishing as the sigmoid colon and rectum.

You may want to refer to an anatomy text for a more in-depth discussion of the internal organs. For now, sense their general position and volume, using your breath to palpate them. The kidneys lie on either side of the spine above the waist. The uterus is deep in the abdomen above the pubic bone.

Now bring your attention to your skeletal structure, as if you were seeing the body with X-ray vision. Extend your right arm over your head and bend to the left, focusing your attention on the bones moving. Repeat this to the other side.

Returning to the first side, initiate the side bend from the skeleton and then Shift your attention to the underlying organs, focusing on elongating the organs on the right side of the body and compressing the organs on the left. Did you go further? How did the quality of the movement change as your focus shifted?

Now initiate the side bend as a movement that arises from the organs. Breathe into and elongate the organs on the right side of the body, letting the skeleton follow. How did this experience differ from the one in which you had your mind on the skeletal system alone?

The organs are the seat of our deepest emotions; we physically experience strong feelings as sensations in the viscera (for example, the butterflies of fear or the tight knot of anger). Therefore, many people find that when they initiate movement from the organ system, the movement seems to arise out of their deepest self—that is, there is not a dualistic sense that the mind is “doing something” to the body. By contrast, when you perceive the body as nothing but a skeleton, it may feel as though your mind is manipulating your body like a puppet on a string.

Now integrate this new awareness of your organs into a simple twisting posture.

Some preliminary suggestions may make your task easier. One of the obstacles to twisting freely is the inability to sit upright with the normal curves of the spinal column intact. When the legs are extended, this problem may be further exaggerated because the hamstrings may pull on the base of the pelvis, causing the back to round (Figure 1: Incorrect). In this position, you are actually sitting on the base of the spine rather than on the sitting bones, and the collapse of the outer body makes it difficult to breathe freely.

To make sitting—and therefore twisting—a little easier, this first variation calls for both legs to be folded. By deactivating the hamstrings, we allow the pelvis to move more freely into an upright position.

Sit cross-legged with the buttocks elevated on a blanket or cushion. Place the right leg so the shin is upright, with the sole of the right foot directly in front of the left ankle. Inhaling fully, allow the abdomen to expand freely. On your exhalation roll the abdomen to the right, guiding the abdomen back against the spine to encourage the twist. Bring your left elbow onto the outside of the right knee (Figure 2).

With each breath, allow the soft inner body to move circularly in the direction of the twist, very much as if you were doing a belly dance. Once the lower torso is turning freely to the right, direct the breath more fully into the right side of the chest. Expanding the right lung with the inhalation, encourage the thoracic spine to move in and up. As you exhale, release the left lung from the center of the chest out into the shoulder, allowing the muscles along the back of the body to follow the changing shape of the lung.

As this occurs, the shoulder blade and then the arm will move further around.

Replace the elbow against the knee as necessary. When you feel you have reached your limit, stay for a few more breaths, simply letting the inhalation and exhalation oscillate the body slightly to and fro. Release on an exhalation and then repeat on the other side.

Now extend both legs in front of you, placing a blanket underneath your buttocks if necessary to create an erect sitting position. Sit with your back one arm’s length from a wall. Bend your right knee, placing the heel of the right foot in line with the sitting bone of the right side of the pelvis. Extend downward through the length of the left leg, simultaneously pressing the right foot down into the floor. Feel how this groundedness through the bones rebounds up through the body as the energy flows through the soft organs and the bones to support the erect carriage of the torso. When you release the downward movement of the legs, notice how the spine sags and the whole torso wilts.

Sense how the movements of the muscles and bones affect the shape of the internal organs, and vice versa.

As you inhale, direct the breath into the mid and upper chest. With each exhalation, successively turn from the lowest part of the belly to the head. Bring your elbow onto the outside of the right knee and place your hand against the wall, making sure that you are far enough from the wall that the shoulder is not elevated toward the ears (Figure 3). Use your arm to lift and support the torso, but do not overpower the soft movements of the inner body by using the arm to forcefully turn the outer muscles. Instead of using the arm as a “dictator,” let your arm become a “guide.” In the same way, wait for the inner body to yield to the movement, then encourage it with the guiding arm.

Take a few more full breaths before releasing and repeating the movement on the second side.

In this exercise you will focus on the contents of the spine—the spinal cord—to bring deeper awareness to your movement. Begin by sitting in Staff Pose (Dandasana) with both legs extended. Bend the left knee and place the heel of the left foot in line with the sitting bone. Now place the left hand immediately behind the left buttock and use it to support the trunk.

Before beginning the twist, take a moment to bring a few central images to mind. Start by bringing your awareness to the contents of the skull. Sense whether the brain is balanced equally between the front and back of the skull. Exiting the brain is the brain stem; then the spinal cord runs through each vertebrae like thread running through a string of beads.

Think of your spinal cord as the tail of your brain and the vertebrae as individual beads, each with its own size and shape.

As you bring your awareness to the brain stem, notice how the spinal cord curves inward so that the cervical vertebrae stack up underneath the head. As you continue your mental journey down the back, the soft spinal cord curves outward, following the convex curve of the thoracic spine. As you move your attention down toward the base of the rib cage, the spinal cord loops back in and the five lumbar vertebrae stack directly under the center of the chest. Continue on down to the massive sacral bone which curves outward and articulates with the two wings of the pelvis.

Having established this anatomical map, begin to sense how the bones of the spine are positioned in relationship to the soft spinal cord. Are there any areas of the spinal cord that feel compressed, perhaps even red and sore from being pressed and rubbed by the bodies of the vertebrae? Are there vertebrae that feel as if they were glued together, or areas where the bones feel rotated or collapsed on one side? Use your breath to gently move your vertebrae as if you were rearranging very precious antique furniture in a room. Adjust the vertebrae so they glide over the spinal cord easily.

As you enter the twist, continue to gauge your movement to avoid any irritation to the spinal cord. (While the brain is insensitive to pain, the outer sheath of the spinal cord is richly supplied with sensory nerve fibers.) Imagine that you are initiating the movement from the level of the spinal cord. If you overpower the spine with the strength of the arm, the result will often be irritation in the spine during the twist and an ache in the back long after your practice is finished.

Once the torso has rotated so the chest is facing the left knee, you can take the “hand lock” by bringing the right arm around the outside of the left shin. Link the fingers or, if possible, hold the left wrist with the right hand. Exhale and draw the hands away from the shoulders, allowing the spine to lengthen strongly upward.

If taking the hand lock compresses the front of the abdomen and collapses the spine, you are moving your skeleton further than the organs can support. Be conscious of using your breath to shape the internal organs. Keep the front of the abdomen open and draw the base of the left rib cage in toward the waist to encourage full spinal extension. Turn the head to look back at the foot of the extended leg (Figure 4). Take a few more breaths and then release. Repeat on the other side.

To clarify the distinction between initiating movement from the inner body and dominating with the outer muscles, you might try the previous exercises again, this time exerting force with the outer body by using the arm as a strong lever. Notice the tone in the muscle tissue when you exert force from the outside, as opposed to the quality when you allow the inner body to give to the movement in its own time. Also notice how the two different ways of initiating movement create different psychological states.

Within each of us is a longing for wholeness. Like the spiraling shape of the twist, our spiritual path must constantly turn back toward the still center within us. The longing to “get somewhere” through yoga is a distortion of our true urge to return back to the undifferentiated, unchanging core from which all life expands.

#8943. Cycling Metrics Guide: What to Measure for Better Rides

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

Confused about all the data? Learn what numbers to track to see your progress and improve your performance.

My favorite metric has always been feel. I trained for two Ironman, including World Championships in Kona and entire mountain bike stage races like Cape Epic and Brasil Ride tracking nothing but time, distance, speed, and how I felt. I’d trained enough with heart rate and power to know how they worked, but I always reverted to feel.

That said, there have certainly been races where I’ve blown up—where the implosion probably could have been prevented had I been watching my watts. And the times I did spend training with power, there’s little question my sessions were more precise and likely more productive. It can be easier to stay on track with training when you have measurable goals and quantifiable sessions.

Today, I strike a compromise between luddite and tech-geek, tracking my resting heart rate and heart rate variability with an Oura ring, and recording heart rate for most rides so I can keep an eye on how fatigued and/or fresh I am.

Ultimately, I think that’s the best process when it comes to using data. Start with the basics, then add on as you get more experience. Most riders end up settling on a handful of metrics they rely on most.

Here, a primer to get you started tracking your cycling metrics.

Obviously, tracking cycling metrics generally means you need a device to capture that data. Most of the metrics, such as speed, distance, time, and elevation, mentioned here can be captured with a GPS-enabled bike computer like a Garmin, Wahoo, Lezyne, or Hammerhead. The deeper you want to dive into the data, the more sensors you need.

Great for: The satisfaction of seeing your pace pick up

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

Your miles per hour (or kilometers per hour, depending on where you live) is a fun metric to track, and it can tell you broadly high much fitter you’re getting. The catch: It’s not very reliable to use in training because so many factors influence it. For example, you may be cranking out World Pro-level wattage but if you’re doing so into a 30-mph block headwind, you’re not going to be setting any land speed records.

Your average speed is best used as an indicator of how your training is going overtime: If you are now consistently averaging 16+ mph on a loop that you used to average 15+ mph, you can see you’re getting fitter and faster.

You can track your average time with and without your stopping time factored into the pace. Most people don’t factor stoppage (or “café time”) in because they want to see moving time only. But if you’re training for a big event like a gravel race, it’s important to know your average speed including that stoppage time, because races often set cut offs based on a 10-mph pace, which includes rest stops. Once you see how long those “short breaks” really are, you can learn to keep them quick and avoid missing time cuts. You’ll also know how fast you need to ride to allow yourself the stoppage time you plan to take.

Great for: Watching your endurance increase

Equipment needed: Any basic bike computer

We all like to see how far we’ve gone, especially on a big ride. Distance can be a motivational metric to track. If you’re averaging 50 to 80 miles a week, can you make it 100? Can you set an annual goal of hitting 5,000 miles or more? When tracking distance, it’s important to take into consideration what type of riding you do. Riding 60 miles on flat roads is very different from 60 miles of singletrack. One might take three to four hours while the other takes the better part of a day.

Distance is also important to track if you’re training for a ride of a specific distance. If you want to ride a century in the fall, you’ll want to work up to it by hitting 50-mile and 75-mile rides as the event approaches.

Great for: Learning pacing for eventsEquipment needed: Any watch will do, but a bike computer can automatically track moving time and stoppage time

Most cyclists train by time because that’s our most finite resource. How much time you have each week to ride determines how to best use that time if your goal is to improve performance. Riders with a tight time budget are best served doing polarized training that emphasizes short, hard interval workouts during the week and longer rides as time permits on the weekend.

Great for: Bragging rights and building strength (hills make you stronger!)

Equipment needed: A GPS enabled bike computer

Elevation gain in cycling is the total amount of feet (or meters) you climb over the course of a ride. Climbing is good training, because your body must work harder in the effort to overcome the pull of gravity. If you’re the kind of rider who routinely avoids inclines, setting climbing goals and tracking elevation can give your cycling fitness a boost. If your goal is to focus on elevations, start by aiming to hit an average of 500 feet per 10 miles. Work up to what some climbing lovers call the “golden ratio” of 1,000 feet of vertical gain per 10 miles of riding.

Equipment needed: Apps like Strava will estimate your calorie burn, but for more accurate data, use a heart rate monitor and/or power meter

A calorie is a unit of energy provided by food. The calorie metric provided on your cycling computer or smartwatch is how many of those units you used to complete your ride. But calorie calculations are an imperfect science.

Some devices will provide estimates based on algorithms, which are just that—estimates. Past research has shown that devices can have a wide margin of error: A Stanford study published in 2017 reported that not one of the seven devices they tested—including the Apple Watch, Fitbit Surge, Mio Alpha 2, Basis Peak, Microsoft Band, PulseOn, and the Samsung Gear S2—delivered an accurate number for calories burned. The most accurate one, the Apple Watch, was off by 27 percent. The least accurate one? Off by 93 percent.

A more recent meta-analysis published in The British Journal of Sports Medicine echoed these findings, indicating that though devices that measure your heart rate along with your movement are more accurate, they all have a pretty significant margin of error.

Apps like GarminConnect, Strava, and other training apps might be a bit better, but they’re not perfect, either, and the number they give you depends heavily on the information you give the app. The more detailed data you input about yourself, such as age, height, weight, gender, and max heart rate, the more accurately their internal algorithms can calculate your calorie burn. Wearing a chest-based heart rate monitor that is synced to your device also helps make your calorie count more accurate.

Ultimately, the best way to know how many calories you burn on a ride is by using a power meter. Power meters measure the work you’re performing and display it in kilojoules, which is a unit of work that takes into account that the human body isn’t 100-percent efficient when turning energy from your fuel stores into physical work, like pedaling a bike.

“Kilojoules and calories burned in cycling convert to a 1:1 ratio,” explains USA Cycling elite coach Daniel Matheny, head coach at Matheny Endurance in Colorado Springs. If your ride file says you performed 800 kJ of work, you can feel confident within a 5-percent margin of error that you burned about 800 calories.

Tracking calories is useful for helping you fuel for rides. Some riders underestimate the number of calories they’ll burn on a three-hour group ride and end up falling off the back on the verge of bonking three quarters of the way through. Properly fueled riders ride faster and happier.

Just note that the goal is not to replace every calorie you’re burning as you ride. Your gut can’t take that. “Replace about half the calories you’re burning per hour for rides lasting longer than three or four hours to keep fuel levels topped off,” says sports physiologist and SkratchLabs founder Allen Lim, Ph.D.

You may also notice that the fitter you become, the fewer calories you burn on a given ride at a given pace. That’s because your body has become more efficient at using oxygen.

Great for: Training leg strength and speed; watching fitness improve for new riders

Equipment needed: A cycling computer and cadence sensor

Cadence is the number of revolutions you spin per minute as you pedal. If you have a cadence sensor you can watch your cadence in real time on your bike computer and track your average cadence for each ride.

It’s debatable how useful it is to track and/or train cadence. Coaches used to recommend athletes aim to pedal 90 rpm, but research doesn’t really show benefits from forcing yourself to do so. In 2019, a team of British researchers found that not only did amateur riders not get any added benefit from high cadence cycling, but they also became less efficient, so they were wasting energy.

Hunter Allen, CEO of Peaks Coaching Group, and author of Training and Racing with a Power Meter explains that your cadence will be determined by two things: your main muscle fiber type and your level of cardiovascular cycling fitness. The balance of those factors (which, of course, can change over time) determine your ideal cadence.

Newer riders tend to pedal more slowly because their cardiovascular system can’t handle the higher heart rate that comes with high cadences. As fitness improves, cadence generally rises.

While you probably don’t need to track your cadence from ride to ride, if you have a cadence sensor, it can help you do cadence drills, such as low gear/high cadence and high gear/low cadence drills that can help build cardiovascular fitness, leg speed, and leg strength.

Great for: Learning what sustainable (and unsustainable) efforts feel like and tracking fitness improvement

Equipment needed: Your heart, lungs, legs, and brain

It doesn’t get any more basic than RPE, your rate of perceived exertion. Put more simply, it's a measure of how hard you feel like you’re working. On a 1 to 10 scale, 1 is coasting along on a flat road with a tailwind, and 10 is full gas, willing yourself not to vomit.

You can also think of this as your “breath analyzer,” because a monitoring your breathing is an easy way to rate your efforts. Your muscles use more oxygen the harder you push, so breathing rate is a direct indication of work. If you’re able to sing and recite poetry, you’re not working very hard. If you’re gasping uncontrollably, you are maxed out.

Research shows RPE works just as well as any scientific equipment for measuring your actual effort at any given time, but it doesn’t tell you much more. For instance, you may be huffing and puffing and battling burning legs, but barely producing any power; or you could be feeling chainless while cranking out major wattage. Though you can train by “feel” alone, you get a more complete picture of your daily sessions and progress if you pair it with other metrics like heart rate or power.

It also takes discipline to train by feel because you have to remain tuned in, and it’s all too easy to slack off when you should be pushing or push too hard on a recovery day.

Great for: Creating specific training zones and tuning into your freshness and/or fatigue

Equipment needed: A heart rate monitor and compatible bike computer or watch

As your effort increases, your heart pumps more oxygen and nutrient-rich blood to fuel your muscles. The result: Your heart rate goes up. Monitoring your heart beats per minute (BPM) with a heart rate monitor will tell you just how hard you’re working.

To use heart rate, you need to first determine your max heart rate (MHR)—or the highest number of BPM you can hit. Forget the generic 220 minus your age formula for determining max heart rate and take a field test instead:

Warm up thoroughly, then do a 10-minute time trial as hard as possible, kicking it into full throttle for the final 60 seconds, aiming to full on sprint the final 20 seconds. Cool down and check your data for MHR. Repeat two more times (with rest days in between) to find your true max. Once you have your max, you can break down various levels of training efforts according to percentages of that number. As you get fitter, you’ll be able to ride faster at lower heart rates.

Overall, heart rate monitoring is an excellent training tool—but there are a few downsides. For one, it’s a little fickle. Your BPM can drift up or down depending on how much coffee you’ve had (caffeine raises it); ambient temperature; your hydration status; your plasma volume; how rested you are; and where you are in your menstrual cycle. It can also drift up within the same ride, especially when it’s hot.

Pairing HR and RPE tracking gives you a more complete picture of your effort. If you’re performing tempo intervals at a target heart rate of 150 BPM and your RPE is around 5, you’re on the money. If you’re performing those same intervals but working at an RPE of 8 to hit that same heart rate, that’s a sign that you’re not recovered and should do an easier workout. There’s also some lag time between the moment you increase intensity and the moment your heart rate reflects it, so it’s not the best tool for high-intensity efforts.

You can monitor your heart rate with a chest strap or wrist-based heart rate monitor via your sports watch. Wrist-based sensors on smartwatches and fitness trackers can be less accurate for cyclists, according to some research. That may be due to the optical sensors having less consistent contact with our wrists as we bend it to grasp our bars.

Great for: The most accurate measure of your effort

Equipment needed: A power meter and a compatible bike computer

Power equals work over time. In cycling, your work rate is described as watts of energy produced: Being able to produce a lot of power for your size makes you faster on the bike. Monitoring your watts with a power meter gives you instant feedback about how hard you’re working.

Power training generally revolves around your functional threshold power, or the wattage you can produce for a one-hour time trial, which is a fundamental benchmark for fitness. A common protocol for determining your FTP is performing a 20-minute time trial and multiplying that average wattage by 0.95, since your hour-long wattage would be about 5 percent lower, according to Allen.

The beauty of power is that it is absolute: You are either producing 350 watts on those hill repeats, or you’re not. If you’re not hitting your intended watts for a given workout, it’s time to rest.

Though power is more precise than heart rate, it’s worthwhile to combine the two, as heart rate represents your body’s response to the work you’re doing. Your heart rate should rise and fall in line with your power output. When your power is low and your heart rate is high, it’s recovery time. If you’re serious about training to the point that you’ve hired a coach, a power meter is a good investment.

Great for: Understanding when you need more recovery time

Equipment needed: An Oura ring, Whoop strap, or specific HRV tracking device

HRV is a relatively new player in the performance tracking sphere. Unlike heart rate, which you watch in real time, HRV is one that you track once a day, preferably first thing in the morning (or if you wear an Oura ring or Whoop strap, you’ll see your average overnight score).

HRV is a good indicator of your recovery and/or readiness. It may seem counterintuitive, but a fit, rested, healthy heart should not beat consistently like a metronome. Instead, it should nimbly respond to input from your sympathetic (fight or flight) and parasympathetic (rest and digest) nervous system.

High variability (reflected in a higher HRV score) shows that you’re ready to go and capable of adapting to your environment and respond to exercise demands to perform well. Low variability between beats can be a sign of stress, fatigue, and inflammation—all things that can follow training too hard with too little recovery.

HRV is specific to each person and naturally declines with age. Though high numbers are considered “better,” high is relative to your own baseline. One person’s high HRV might be 125 while another’s high might be 55.

Referenced regularly, HRV scores will help you track fitness gains. For example, you’ll typically see HRV measurements decrease (become more negative) during long, heavy training blocks. Then you should see a rebound, where your HRV is significantly higher, after a recovery period. An upward trend over time means you’re getting fitter. A downward trend means you’re training too hard and or under too much stress without proper rest and recovery. When using HRV, it’s important not to put too much weight on a single day’s reading, but rather to look at trends and averages over a few days.

You can buy individual HRV monitors like straps and finger clip sensors, but if you’re going to track HRV, you should also track resting heart rate, sleep, and training load and/or activity levels, so you can put it into context. So, a device like a Whoop strap or Oura ring are the way to go, because they automatically put HRV into context of the whole picture. (If you work with a coach, they can as well).

Do you need to track HRV to become a better rider? Of course not. You can generally tell when you need a rest day by feel. But if you routinely train hard and like to dial in your training and lifestyle habits for optimum recovery and training readiness, this is a useful metric to use. It can be especially helpful if you’re trying to establish healthy habits like cutting back on alcohol and getting more sleep, because those types of lifestyle factors show up quickly in HRV scores.

All this measuring and monitoring doesn’t do much good unless you apply it to specific training purposes—that is, training at different effort levels to build specific types of fitness. That’s where training zones come in. Different coaches break down training zones differently, but in general you’ll see effort levels spread out over five to seven zones that range from recovery to max effort. For example, here are five classic training zones:

You need to ride easy so your body can heal, adapt, and get stronger and fitter. Zone 1 rides should feel ridiculously easy. Your only goal is to boost your circulation and promote repair and recovery. These rides hover at one or two on the RPE scale.

Zone 2 is all about aerobic effort. Endurance rides require enough energy to feel like exercise, but still let you carry a conversation, cruise for hours, and enjoy the ride. These efforts stimulate mitochondrial growth and build capillaries and fat-burning capacity. Zone 2 rides are done at an RPE of three to four.

Efforts in Zone 3 are just above your comfort level, so you’re breathing faster and working harder than you would on a typical aerobic, endurance ride. You’re not working so hard, however, that you can’t sustain your effort for a long period of time. Steady Zone 3 tempo efforts improve your body’s ability to clear and use lactic acid, so they also help raise your lactate threshold. They’re done at an RPE of five to six.

If VO2 max is your roof, lactate threshold—the point at which you start working anaerobically—is your drop ceiling. Training in Zone 4, which is right at that point, helps you hit higher intensities before you bump into that overhang. These efforts are done at an RPE of seven to eight.

To raise your VO2max, the maximum amount of oxygen your body can use, you need to push yourself as far into the red as you can go. Zone 5 efforts are done full throttle—a nine to 10 on the RPE scale. Because they’re so hard, they’re also very short, generally lasting three to five minutes.

Here is a sample of basic training zones that incorporate the metrics above. Some coaches will break these down and expand them further or use other metrics such as percent of lactate threshold heart rate as a guide.

#8942. How Runner’s World Training Plans Helped Four Runners Crush the New York City Marathon

Their stories will inspire you to train for your best marathon.

Among the more than 61,000 runners who crossed the finish line of the 2026 TCS New York City Marathon were 18 Runner’s World+ members who were part of the Race With Runner’s World+ team. Two were first-time marathoners while 16 others set big goals, such as adding to their World Marathon Major collection and hitting new PRs. No matter their specific ambition, some team members used these Runner’s World+ training plans to power themselves to the Central Park finish line.

Whatever your goal distance and time, you can find a plan by exploring our full training plan collection, including the ones our members used to return to the marathon, earn a sixth star, and run a PR.

🏃‍♀️ Want to run some of the best races in the country with us? Bookmark our Race With Runner’s World+ program page, which gives Runner’s World+ members of all backgrounds and levels a chance at free entry into select races.

Prior to New York, 46-year-old Erin Dewalt ran her last marathon in 2022, a race that she described as a “disaster.” Then, she finished in more than four hours and had an overall rough race day experience.

After a four-year marathon hiatus, Dewalt knew she needed a smart training plan to ensure she would arrive prepared for the NYC Marathon start line. The RW Break 3:45 plan aligned well with her weekly training volume of around four runs per week. For inspiration, she printed the calendar and stuck it to her fridge, checking off completed runs and moving workouts as needed.

The result for Dewalt in the Big Apple? A 3:26:18 marathon performance—breaking the 3:45 barrier by nearly 20 minutes. “I was spot on [with hitting my goal],” Dewalt said after crossing the finish line. “I wanted to enjoy it and have fun but also run around three and a half hours.”

Like Dewalt, Scott Shellabarger printed a Runner’s World training plan, but he used the Break 3:15 plan. In fact, he used it for two races: the NYC Marathon in November and the Flying Pig Marathon in his hometown of Cincinnati, Ohio, in May. “I actually used it for the last marathon I ran, for the Flying Pig, and that’s where I got my PR at,” Shellabarger said. “The training plans are fantastic.”

Not only did the plan help him set a personal best of 3:18:33 at Flying Pig, but it also helped him earn his Six Star Medal in New York and score a 2028 Boston Marathon qualifying time for his age group. Though he didn’t quite break 3:15 with his 3:21:27 performance, it marked his second-fastest marathon to date.

With a hectic schedule as a coach, Courtney Sobanski knew she needed a training plan that could fit into her everyday life. With our 3-Day training plan, Sobanski managed workouts successfully around other responsibilities—and remained injury-free. Our 3-Day plan features three key workouts a week—and any other days of easy running or cross-training you complete count as extra credit.

At the New York City Marathon, Sobanski crossed the finish line in 4:19:09 and told Runner’s World that she showed herself she could still run strong following foot surgery two years ago. “I’m just overcome with emotion that I actually did it and I can [run marathons] again,” Sobanski said following her race.

Ashley Osburn, 41, used the Break 4:30 plan to have every part of her training block mapped out in front of her—intervals, hills, tempo runs, long runs. Osburn said the plan made workouts approachable, and she appreciated the two weekly rest days built into the schedule for better recovery.

Though she didn’t quite reach her sub-4:30 goal in New York due to fueling missteps, Osburn intends to take another shot at the time barrier again in the future. “I will absolutely use [the training plan] again for my next marathon,” she said.

All of our Race With Runner’s World+ members had different goals and training plans pushing them toward the NYC finish line. But they all had a common shared experience of relishing the ecstatic crowds and infectious energy along the course through the five boroughs. “The crowd support all the way through was just amazing,” Dewalt said.

#8941. Don’t Let a Flat Tire End Your Ride. Here’s What I Carry in My Ride-Rescue Kit

A practical guide to building a flat kit that gets you home without overloading your bike.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

There are so many options out there when setting up a flat tire kit. During my time in bike shops I sold every flat kit you could imagine—from the basic prepackaged flat repair kits to repair kits that could fix almost anything on the bike. When you have the right pieces of gear, it can make the difference between an easy roadside fix and finding a plan B to get home.

Building the right kit can make the difference between fixing the bike mid-ride and needing an unexpected pickup. One key is bringing the things you need and not what you don’t—then knowing how to use the tools in your kit.

Even on bikes you’ve had for a while it can be worth revisiting what’s sitting in your flat pack. Below I’ll walk you through what’s in my basic flat kit, why I pick those pieces, and why you should intermittently check out your flat pack to prevent any roadside surprises.

The tire levers are the foundation of any good flat repair kit—after all, you won’t be able to fix a flat very well if you can’t get the tire off and back on. I’ve gone through many different lever options over the years in my own flat kits, as well as from my time running a bike shop. The tire levers I swear by are the Pedro’s yellow tire levers. They are burly enough to be reliable and durable—I’m rarely worried about snapping a Pedro’s lever even on a tight tire.

The one thing many people don’t think about with levers is that sometimes you drop them or put them down when you’re trying to manage the roadside repair. The Pedro’s levers are easy to find thanks to their bright yellow color.

One runner-up is the tire lever from Muc-Off. They are similar in size, durability, and come in bright and easy to find colors. Personally I have not had the same amount of time using Muc-Off levers compared to the Pedro’s levers. One final tip: don’t use metal levers. Yes, they are burly, but they can easily damage rims when trying to get a tire off—especially carbon.

The traditional tube you may have gotten the last time you stopped in your local shop while picking up a tube to fix a flat at home is a great option to put in your flat pack, but there are other options. TPU and latex tubes are popular because of their light weight and small packed size.

I typically go with a standard tube on most of my flat kits. This is because I typically ride all year round and some of those lighter and more packable materials for tubes are more sensitive to temperature. If you’re a fair-weather rider, however, it can be worth considering a TPU or latex tube. Just remember to double-check that both the tube and valve size are correct for the wheels you are using.

One note on checking out your tubes: check to make sure the tube is in good condition every few months. I was on a ride recently where someone got a flat and his multitool was against the tube in his saddle bag. The multitool rubbed a hole into the side of the tube making it useless. He said he had not inspected that tube in at least a year. Luckily we had an extra tube for him and could keep rolling, but a quick check could have prevented him pulling a tube from someone else’s flat kit.

Similar to tire levers, I’ve used many different inflators over the years. My favorites to use are either the PDW CO2 inflator or the Muc-Off Inflator. These two options are durable and are easy to use with gloves on—which is especially helpful as we get into some cooler temperatures.

I carry two cans of CO2 because I’ve run into several experiences before where one ends up not being enough. It could be because I used one to try to add a burst of air in the hopes my tubeless system would fill the hole with sealant and I could go on my way. I’ve also had user error experiences where I simply didn’t get the canister on correctly and most or all of the air rushed out of the canister. In any case, they don’t take up much space, but having a backup is a key piece of the flat kit.

There are other inflation options you can go with too. Electronic pumps have been growing in popularity over the last few years, with test editor Dan Chabanov recently calling out the Cycplus AS2 Ultra Electric Inflator as his inflator of choice. I typically add a frame-mounted pump on longer rides, because these can’t run out of battery and as long as you can still pump you won’t run out of available air.

You’d be surprised what you can fix with a few zip ties. I’ve used these packable and inexpensive additions to fix issues like broken bottle cage bolts and broken cable and housing guides. I’ve had friends who have reattached things like derailleurs and saddle bags with a few strategically placed zip ties.

When I ride I typically carry a $10 bill and a single dollar bill. I know $11 seems like a random amount of money to carry on the bike. But the single and the ten serve two different purposes. A single dollar bill works as a great tire boot if you have a large gash in your tire. Simply put the dollar bill inside the tire against the gash before putting the tube in. If you run tubeless you can apply a little sealant from inside the tire to the dollar bill to help it stick better against the tire. Then when you inflate your tube, the pressure of the tube inside the tire will keep the dollar bill in place. The dollar bill will protect the tube from the elements and the road surface outside the tire.

The ten-dollar bill is your backup plan. I’ve been on rides before where I underestimated the amount of hydration and nutrition I needed to get through an effort. Having a few dollars for a gas station or convenience store refuel stop has dragged me out of the hole more than once. Most places these days take digital forms of payment like Apple Pay, but if you’re riding in more remote areas cash can be king.

A multitool that has the basic Allen keys and screwdriver that you’ll need is essential. If it has sizes 4, 5, and 6 you’ll be able to take care of most roadside fixes or adjustments you might ride into.

I personally like to bring a multitool with a chain breaker because I’ve had to fix a chain more than once on a ride. If fixing a chain is something you want to be prepared for on your ride, consider bringing a quick link that is compatible with your chain. They are another small and relatively inexpensive addition to your flat kit that can save plenty of headaches. A broken chain doesn’t have to be the end of your ride if you have the tools and the knowledge to piece it back together.

Different bikes have different ways to carry all this stuff. Some bikes have internal frame storage, some saddles have integrated mounts for certain bags, and some bikes have dropper posts that are only compatible with select saddle bags. On really short road rides I’ve even just thrown the basics of my flat kit in a jersey pocket. Personally, I typically put my flat repair kit into a frame bag, saddle bag, or utilize the internal frame storage so I can keep the extra weight and bulk off my body. If you have any essentials in your flat kit that I don’t include in mine let me know in the comments below.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.
