#8928. What Runners Need to Know About Rhabdo

After a tragic death in the running community, doctors want runners to know the risk factors for the condition.

Shortly after the New York City Marathon, tragic news broke: A 24-year-old runner, Rachel Apa, collapsed on the course and died in the hospital after doctors worked for six hours to save her life, according to the New York Times. Apa’s father told NYT the cause of death was rhabdomyolysis (a.k.a. rhabdo).

The news is shocking and saddening—as well as unsettling. Questions are popping up from runners on social media as to how something like this could happen to a young woman who was reportedly a former Division I field hockey player at Bucknell University and had spent months training for the marathon.

To help answer some of those questions, we talked to doctors to explain what runners need to know about rhabdo, and how to stay safe.

First, know that rhabdo is relatively rare and dying from it is even rarer. Approximately 26,000 cases of rhabdomyolysis are reported annually in the United States, and the mortality rate starts at 10 percent but may go up to 50 percent in severe cases.

In short, rhabdo is a breakdown of muscle that in and of itself is not life-threatening. In fact, Derek M. Fine, MD, a nephrologist at Johns Hopkins Medicine, says that if you were to test creatine kinase (a.k.a. CK, a blood marker of muscle breakdown) in marathon runners after the race, “most” of them would show elevated levels of the enzyme.

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention says that multiple CK tests are the only way to accurately identify rhabdo, though. Normal CK is between 20 and 200 U/L, but rhabdo is diagnosed when it reaches five times the upper limit.

“There’s always a little bit of muscle breakdown and the reason is because, at least in [a] marathon, you’re using the muscles so much that at some point they can run out of an energy supply,” Fine says, adding that the mitochondria can't keep up and make enough of what’s called ATP (adenosine triphosphate), which is your primary source of energy.

Rhabdo becomes dangerous when it becomes more severe. As muscle tissue breaks down, the body can release harmful substances into the bloodstream, including myoglobin, a protein that can damage the kidneys, and excessive amounts of potassium.

As for myoglobin, the protein can get “stuck” in the kidney and cause kidney failure or injury at various levels, Fine says. “It can be quite severe, but that usually takes a little bit of time to manifest,” he explains.

Fine says that high levels of potassium are probably a bigger risk than myoglobin. “When the muscle cells break up, you get a very large release of potassium into the bloodstream and that potassium then can cause cardiac arrhythmias,” he says. This can cause kidney failure (your kidneys are the organ tasked with getting rid of extra potassium) or potentially sudden cardiac arrest.

“Under normal circumstances, if it’s happening slowly and you’ve got decent kidneys, you pee the potassium out and it never gets that high in the blood,” he says. “If there's severe rhabdo and you have a huge amount of muscles breaking down, you can release a ton of potassium and your body can't get rid of it fast enough.”

In addition to the rapid release of these substances, rhabdo can sometimes lead to other issues that resemble sepsis or even multisystem organ failure, Fine says.

Still, rhabdo is not a common underlying cause of cardiac arrest, says Lili Barouch, MD, director of sports cardiology at Johns Hopkins Medicine and an endurance athlete herself. However, it can lead to abnormal heart rhythms due to severe electrolyte problems, primarily high potassium. And as Fine also explains, kidney failure (as well as other organ failure) can result in cardiac problems, she says.

It’s not just running that can increase risk of rhabdo—any heavy exercise can do damage to muscles, Barouch says, particularly exertional rhabdomyolysis. In fact, Fine says that there have been incidents of rhabdo reported in CrossFit athletes for this reason. Whether it’s a marathon or weight lifting, it’s in high-effort situations that the muscle breakdown can accelerate rapidly and lead to problems.

As for running, while training does induce microscopic damage to muscles that later repairs in a stronger way—a positive outcome—many people push harder in a marathon. “For a race, you’re usually going at a much higher level of effort and you’re really pushing yourself to your limit,” Barouch says.

This can be true for athletes of any level, but people who aren’t as highly trained who push really hard on race day may be at higher risk, Fine says. “The most common reason [for getting rhabdo] is you’ve got someone who overdoes it and who wasn’t trained enough,” he says. (This was not necessarily the case with Apa, just a potential risk factor for runners in general.)

Another risk factor is dehydration, Barouch says. “If someone’s dehydrated, the amount of those muscle breakdown products [your body produces] that can become toxic to the kidneys starts to really go up. You're unable to clear the toxins out of your body fast enough and that can cause more damage,” she says.

On the flip side, good hydration can help flush the myoglobin from the kidneys, per Fine. But, he points out that there’s a delicate balance between being over- and underhydrated: “While you’re running a marathon, your kidneys are getting messages from your brain to hold on to water, so if you keep putting water in there, the water dilutes out the sodium in the blood and you can get hyponatremia,” he says. The key: Drink to thirst and take electrolytes during a long or hot race, Fine says.

Carbohydrates could help as well. “Part of rhabdo could be if you’re not giving enough carbohydrates and energy [to your body], you can't make ATP [the energy currency you need to perform] and that’s where the muscle could break down,” Fine says.

Another factor for marathon runners is environmental conditions. “If it’s a particularly hot day, for example, that seems to be a big risk factor,” Fine says. In fact, there was an unusually large incidence (24 cases) of exertional rhabdomyolysis at the 2022 NYC Marathon, per a study in Nephron Clinical Practice, likely associated with the “unseasonably high heat and humidity” on race day, per the authors.

Younger runners may actually be at higher risk of rhabdo, likely because they’re more inclined to take risks and push harder than the older population, Fine says, potentially ignoring signs of rhabdo.

There’s also a genetic component to rhabdo, Fine says. So, if you have had rhabdo before, or have a family member who has had rhabdo, it could be worth looking into your own risk more closely.

It’s not super common, but genetic tests look at certain markers that might suggest someone is more susceptible to rhabdo. “It’s not like you're going to say, ‘Okay, I’m going to run a marathon, I’m going to go do prescreening genetic testing,’” Fine says. “But in someone who may have had this before, even if they said, ‘Well, I did CrossFit and I got rhabdo and I'm now going to try to run a marathon,’ that sort of person may be worth checking.”

Finally, certain medications (including statins and certain antidepressants) and underlying conditions (like McArdle disease and Duchenne muscular dystrophy) might predispose someone to rhabdo, Barouch says.

The experts agree that signs of rhabdo can be hard to identify because aches are pretty much unavoidable when running a marathon. Still, severe pain in the working muscles (e.g., the legs) is a red flag, Fine says, as are muscle weakness and swelling.

“Of course during a marathon, people tend to have muscle pain, but if it’s much more severe than usual or much more severe than expected,” that’s what to watch for, per Barouch. Severe muscle soreness after the race is also something to keep an eye on, she adds.

Another thing to look out for is urine color. “What one might see early on is very sort of dark orange, rust-colored urine, and that’s the myoglobin coming out,” Fine says. “If someone’s got muscle pain and their urine’s orange, they probably want to go and get checked out and maybe get hydrated and get a CK level checked in an emergency room.”

Per the CDC, the earlier you get treated, the more likely you’ll recover without long-lasting or permanent health effects, so don’t wait if you suspect you have rhabdo.

At the end of the day, it comes down to listening to your body. “As endurance athletes especially, we tend to push ourselves really hard for a race because we have personal goals, time goals, things like that, but you still have to listen to your body,” Barouch says.

If something feels off, don’t ignore it. “Marathons are not comfortable to run for anybody, but if your muscles seem extremely painful or if you start to have other symptoms, if you’re having breathing problems, chest problems, things like that, that seem out of the ordinary, [do] not ignore those warning signs either for rhabdo or another medical condition that might be building up,” Barouch says.

#8927. The Best Gravel Riding Pockets in the U.S.—Including One Unexpected Sleeper Spot

These gravel pockets deliver rail trails, rugged climbs, epic events, and one sleeper pick.

I’ve been invited on gravel rides that range from a mix of road and well-maintained rail trail to rides where I wished I had a hardtail mountain bike. Admittedly, I’ve been the ringleader on more than one occasion for a solidly underbiked ride that was listed as a gravel ride.

There are many people I talk to who say they have the best places to ride gravel. Some pride themselves on challenging and chunky gravel roads, while other places have gravel rides with a 10,000-foot view. And how each rider defines gravel will be different from person to person.

The definition of gravel typically exists between well-maintained packed gravel that feels like a road to singletrack that has some gravel between the more technical bits. Many areas of the country may boast one great gravel quality, but this list compiles the places that check off more than a few boxes.

At this point, it’s clear gravel riding is here to stay, but the challenge lies in deciding where to ride first. Our list has the best gravel riding pockets in the country and can serve as your checklist for 2027. The last destination on the list is a sleeper you shouldn’t miss.

The New York Times featured a run-down of the best spots in the U.S. for gravel biking, so you know it’s now officially mainstream. Their list included Northwest Arkansas, namely Bentonville—in the heart of the Ozark Mountains—which has become known as a gravel (and all things biking) hub. That’s thanks in large part to the Walton family. The Waltons own Walmart and run the Walton Family Foundation, which has always prioritized bikes and outdoor recreation.

If you’re in the area, there are endless ways to spend a day on a bike. According to the NYT, Chuck Campbell, an environmental manager for a wastewater recycling company, has designed several epic loops that together make up the 1,200-mile Arkansas High Country Route, a mix of paved and unpaved roads that launched in 2019.

Colorado might be home to the unique gravel races of any state, but if you’re looking for gravel events you can likely find one in just about any state these days. Steamboat Springs launched SBT GRVL in 2019. They’ve since grown to be one of the most inclusive events out there, with all kinds of training ride opportunities, and partnerships with inclusive cycling groups such as All Bodies on Bikes and Ride for Racial Justice.

If you’re looking for a quieter way to enjoy Colorado gravel, check out Nederland, a quaint mountain town 30 minutes outside of Boulder. There are probably more gravel roads in and around Nederland than paved, and almost all of them take you to excellent cafes and snack shops to recharge. Nederland to Gold Hill with a homemade slice of pie from the Gold Hill Store is tough to beat.

If you’re looking for a way to escape the cold in the coming months, Arizona offers tons of gravel-friendly riding. Many of the multiuse trails around the Phoenix State Parks can be connected for some hearty loops. AZ Gravel Rides has compiled an excellent list of gravel adventures in all areas of the state.

Patagonia, Arizona, has become a not-so-secret winter escape for gravel lovers lately. Located in the Patagonia Mountains, it’s got a desert mountain feel, with plenty of climbing and lots of sandy roads with incredible views. The area is expansive, so you can ride all day without seeing anyone. According to the NYT, “a new edition in the expanding “Gravel Adventure Field Guide” series focuses on routes in Patagonia and surrounding Santa Cruz County.”

And on the East Coast, Vermont can’t be beat. Most people in Vermont will probably tell you that they prefer dirt roads to paved ones. There’s something nice about a slower pace. Seven Days VT claims that Vermont has 8,579 miles of unpaved roads, compared to 7,182 miles of paved roads.

The VTXL is a 300-mile route that stretches from Canada to Massachusetts via 90 percent dirt and gravel roads. Former WorldTour rider turned adventure/gravel pro Ted King is currently bikepacking the route that he’s done before in a single push. This time he’s documenting the summer’s flooding that ravaged the state. “Heartbreaking but with short memories, we want to help bring attention to just how devastating it was and continues to be as Vermont rebuilds,” he posted to social media.

The gravel in Vermont is extensive, but make sure you tie in a climb up the road dubbed, “the steepest paved mile in the U.S..” Lincoln Gap may be known for having the steepest paved mile in the US, but the descent down from the climb is high quality gravel. Just a heads up—if you’re a fan of breweries, then plan for more stops than you would normally expect.

When I think of a great area for riding gravel there are some factors that the location needs to have. Hard gravel climbs with ripping descents, some views while you catch your breath on top of the climbs, and something for everyone to ride—regardless of skill level, are a few things that top my list. Northern Pennsylvania may not be among the top areas for gravel riding for many people, but it should be.

Rail trails like the Pine Creek Rail Trail leave an option for anyone to get out on gravel in this area, but there are plenty of options for the seasoned cyclists as well. Events like Endless Mountains, Unpaved Pennsylvania, and Lu Lacka Wyco Hundo boast routes from 50 miles to 430 miles long. For context—the 115-mile route of Endless Mountains had over 12,000 feet of climbing. A large majority of the route was on gravel with very little stretches of paved country roads.

While the views from the top of the hills are beautiful its worth noting you don’t have the vistas of other locations like Colorado or Arizona. The area makes up for it’s lack of high alpine overlooks or desert landscapes with tough, punchy gravel climbs and positive vibes from the locals. Make sure this unexpected gravel honey hole ends up on your destination list for 2027. If you think I missed a spot (or have somewhere I should add for my 2027 ride list), then drop it in the comments below.

Micah Ling is a freelance writer who lives in the mountains of Colorado. She splits her free time between mountain biking and trail running.

Jason Griffin is Bicycling's Senior Health and Fitness Editor, bringing more than a decade of fitness experience and years in the cycling industry to every story. A former personal trainer and bike shop manager, he's lined up for crits, tackled enduros, but prefers getting lost on multi-day bikepacking adventures. Lately though, his toughest balancing act has been fitting trainer rides between family life and the next adventure.

#8926. Warrior 2 Teaches You to Balance Effort and Surrender

(Photo: Andrew Clark; Design in Canva by Laura Harold)

In Yoga Journal’s Archives series, we share a curated collection of articles originally published in past issues beginning in 1975. This article about how to do Warrior 2 Pose first appeared in the May-June 2000 issue of Yoga Journal. Find more of our Archives here.

Over two millennia ago, one of the most essential teachings of yoga was given on a battlefield, of all places. As recounted in the Bhagavad Gita, Arjuna, the consummate warrior, becomes paralyzed with doubt and fear just as he is about to be called to action. Luckily for him, his chariot driver happens to be none other than the god Krishna, who proceeds to reveal to Arjuna the teachings of yoga to liberate him from his confusion.

In my favorite translation of the Gita, by the late scholar/teacher Eknath Easwaran (Nilgiri Press, 1985), Krishna defines yoga as “wisdom in action”—yogah karmasu kausalam (II.50). He guides Arjuna to reflect upon the source of his actions and find his internal center, where he is free from the fluctuations of the mind.

Many centuries later Mahatma Gandhi would take these teachings of the Gita as guiding principles for his life.

Gandhi saw the battlefield as a metaphor for our internal conflicts and Arjuna as the archetypal warrior within—one who sees through illusions to the truth and is able to act with courage and unwavering focus. Perhaps as a beginning yoga student, you have already encountered a glimpse of this warrior spirit in the standing pose Virabhadrasana II (or Vira II for short). In the deep lunge and open arms of this Warrior Pose variation, there is a challenging intensity—a marked contrast to the images of yoga as a passive practice intended for relaxation.

You may ask, “Why is there a Warrior Pose, when yoga is a practice of nonviolence?”

As a strong pose, Virabhadrasana II can teach modern yogis a lot about the dynamics of bringing wisdom into the actions of our everyday lives. It is a powerful pose, no doubt, but as you explore the pose’s alignment and inner attitude, the heart of the peaceful warrior begins to reveal itself.

As we go about our daily lives, we often speak of feeling “off-centered” or of needing to “get centered.” Being “centered” is a feeling of being balanced and at ease on all levels—physically, emotionally, mentally, spiritually.

It is the clear space of awareness from which the wise action within any moment can be found.

To find your center in Virabhadrasana II—the place where your energy is distributed evenly, without bias—start by grounding yourself within Tadasana (Mountain Pose). The training of a spiritual warrior begins here as you let go of any external distractions and bring your awareness to your core.

When you feel your mind settle within the relaxed steadiness of Tadasana, then prepare to begin Virabhadrasana II. Consciously step your feet apart in a wide stance (4 to 5 feet), with your heels aligned parallel to one another. Pivot your left foot out to a 90-degree angle and pivot your right foot in to a 45-degree angle. Plant your feet like roots, connecting through all of the corners of your feet while lifting through the arches.

To focus on the leg work of Virabhadrasana II first, keep your arms relaxed at your sides. Slowly bend your left knee until it comes directly over your ankle. Now explore the feeling of your weight. Is all of your weight in your front leg? Lunge deeper into your left leg and then shift your weight into your back leg to feel the extremes, and then try to find the balance point.

Let your left hip sink to draw you deeper into the lunge, but keep your right leg firm, inner thigh lifting, and outer edge of your right foot reaching into the ground. As your legs develop stamina and your hips open, you can begin to explore coming into a right angle with your front leg as if you are balancing something on your thigh.

Once you find the place where your weight is evenly distributed through your legs and hips, bring your awareness to your torso. Are you collapsing into your lower back? Find your vertical center by turning your tailbone toward the earth. Without tension, lift your lower belly, the seat of your power, towards the spine. This action will awaken your center, so you can begin to extend out of your lower back and spread your chest open. Now balance your rib cage directly over your pelvis. Is your torso turning towards the left leg? Draw your right side and the top of your right thigh back to feel yourself opening out from the center.

Keep scanning your body to feel where you are losing awareness and balance. Change sides and explore Virabhadrasana II to find that even flow of energy—north, south, east, and west—throughout the pose.

As a metaphor for living, yoga can help us see how unnecessary tension within our actions shifts us off-center. To maintain Warrior Pose, we often harden our eyes, hold our breath, or shrug our shoulders. Try Virabhadrasana II again on the left side, setting up your foundation from your center. Slowly raise your arms up to shoulder height, keeping your shoulder blades pressing into and down your back. Now, turn your gaze (drishti) to the middle finger of your left hand.

Like a Zen archer spotting a bull’s-eye, who practices just holding a bow for two years before ever releasing an arrow, find balance within your focus by becoming inwardly detached.

Let the backs of your eyes look inside while you stay totally present. Feel the power of your energy radiating freely from your center. Find the balance between working to your full potential and completely relaxing, mirroring the effortless stillness of an eagle hovering over a current of wind.

As you explore this dance between being active and receptive, you can contemplate Krishna’s paradoxical teaching, “One who can see action within inaction and inaction within action is the wisest among all beings.”

As you look out from this still point and open your inner ears, you may hear your internal warrior teacher giving you insights to bring you into balance not only in this moment, but in your life as a whole. Like Arjuna as Krishna whispered over his shoulder, you may be given confidence to face your fears, courage to move forward, compassion to embrace another, and wisdom to surrender to the one who holds the reins.

#8925. I Added 10 More Miles a Week to Marathon Training—and Seriously Felt the Difference at Mile 20. Here’s How to Do It Effectively.

How a modest mileage bump helped one marathoner finish stronger, feel better, and build confidence.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

4:09:48. That was my finish time at this year’s New York City Marathon. It was also—to the second—my finish time in the same race last year.

Putting aside the wildness of that (but what does it mean?) I learned a few lessons as I cruised through the five boroughs for the seventh time.

Specifically, although I ran the exact same time, my splits looked quite different. I ran the latter miles faster and they felt easier this year. And that comes down to one key training adjustment I made: adding more overall mileage to my week.

Here’s how and why I maximized my volume during this training cycle, and how it paid off in my strongest finish yet (even if not a PR).

I ran the London Marathon in April, and both New York and Sydney last year, using an artificial intelligence training app. I programmed in that I wanted to run three days a week so I could continue to strength train two to three days a week as well. Plus, I walk quite a bit as someone who lives in New York City (around four to five miles a day on top of any running).

But then I reported on a series of articles about durability for Runner’s World and I started thinking more about total weekly mileage and how much I had (or had not) been doing. Turns out, I peaked around 30 to 35 miles for all three of those marathons. It made me realize there was room for growth.

When I got the opportunity to run New York again this year, I figured out how high I could go mileage-wise without upping my risk for injury.

I started by talking to Andrew Kastor, head coach of the Asics Mammoth Track Club. Before our call, I sent him the training plan I planned to follow for this upcoming training cycle: the Runner’s World Break Four Hours plan. (I also intended to continue strength training twice a week.)

The peak week mileage for that plan: 48 miles, with at least four days a week of running. This may not seem like a ton to people who swear by super high mileage, but it is a steep increase relative to my previous builds. “Between 32 and 50 is night and day,” Kastor says. “You’re going to notice a big difference in your staying power after mile 20.”

Importantly, I built a pretty solid base before starting the training plan 16 weeks out from race day and felt ready to jump into week one when the time came. This plan also leverages mileage ranges, rather than firm numbers, allowing me to further customize it.

Kastor likes the approach of mileage ranges and uses it with many of his athletes. “It kind of takes a little bit of the edge off or the pressure off,” he says, because you can choose the lower end of the range if you’re feeling fatigued.

He also advised me to add in the optional up-to-three-mile run in my plan every other week (where you see 0 to 3 miles). “It’ll be worth it the last mile of the race or the last two miles of the race [when] you’re able to hold that 9:07 pace or that nine flat pace,” he says.

Kastor encouraged me to pay attention to how I was feeling as the training stacked up, and to pull back if I noticed symptoms of overtraining, like an elevated resting heart rate, reduced heart rate variability, or subjective measures like excessive fatigue or feeling flat in workouts. “If [the] legs are not bouncing back week after week, then that’s a sign of overtraining and that you need to pull back and not just pull back with mileage, but take two days off to let your legs recover and heal up,” he says.

I actually felt great throughout my training, which I also attribute to switching up my strength training a bit under the guidance of my physical therapist (I focused more on heavier weight and much less volume, while adding isometrics for tendon health.) Mentally, I also started looking more forward to my running days versus my off days, which is likely due to the fact that I was running more regularly.

In addition to watching for signs of overtraining, Kastor also emphasized the importance of recovery and nutrition when increasing mileage. “In order to do more mileage, you have to sleep well and eat well,” he says.

I focused specifically on eating more carbs than I ever have in training before. (I recently realized I was so focused on protein that I was coming up short on carbs.) As for sleep, I’m always pretty protective of that. So I just kept doing what I was doing: aiming for eight to nine hours a night.

Per Kastor’s suggestion, I also committed to a sports massage every other week during my training, and used the Therabody JetBoots PRO Plus immediately after long runs and occasionally in the evenings on other days. (I feel like they relax my whole nervous system before bed.)

Modern running shoes can also help you handle more time on your feet, Kastor explains. “Generally, because people can handle a little bit more volume with the cushion of the shoes, they’re not breaking down as much,” he says.

I trained in a higher cushioned shoe—the Asics Gel-Nimbus 28—which is known for its premium cushioned, long-lasting ride, according to Runner’s World reviewers. It provided me with a high-energy return and support for the extra miles.

When I spoke to experts in durability about how to increase it for late-race performance, they told me that weekly mileage plays a major role. Research, too, backs up the importance of volume, stating long runs of at least 90 minutes and higher training volumes overall improve durability. And other research suggests more volume (especially easy miles) can lead to faster marathon finish times.

“We start where the athlete is with their fitness and then we progress upward because volume is king,” Kastor says. “More is better as long as you stay healthy.”

He adds that there’s something about the repetition of running frequently that seems to help, citing his wife, marathon Olympic bronze medalist Deena Kastor, as an example. At one point, she was running upward of 140 miles, hitting 13 runs a week, he says. “She would wake up from a nap and be really sleepy, rubbing her eyes, lace up her shoes, and go for a run,” he says. “I think what’s overlooked generally is the role of the nervous system and [how it] plays into the efficiency of running mechanics. If you [run] over and over and over and over again, then you get really, really good at it.”

So, you know I did not PR after adding more mileage to my training plan. But! Take a look at the times for the final four miles in 2025 versus 2026:

I was clearly significantly stronger during the latter miles this year than I was last year, and it was amazing to see and feel that difference. In 2025, I’m honestly surprised I was able to hold the paces I did—I remember feeling pretty wiped, which is why I held back some this time. This year, I felt like I was cruising down 59th Street on the way to mile 25, and even later in the day, I felt good enough to walk almost a mile to dinner and back home.

I felt so strong at the end of this year’s marathon that I know the “mistake” I made was to not trust my training earlier in the race. I was so afraid that I would run out of steam if I held the 8:47 pace I hit at miles 4 and 5 that I pulled back.

So for me, the race was much more of a mental one than a physical one. Now I just have to trust that next time, I can hold faster paces earlier on and still finish strong.

At the end of the day, I realize that I was so focused on my physical training plan and even nutrition that I didn’t think about the psychology of it all. Because I’d run all my long runs at a much easier pace (with the exception of a handful that called for some tempo miles in the middle), I kind of freaked out at the idea of running 26 miles at a 9:00 pace. Now, I truly believe I can. And more mileage is definitely a big part of why.

#8924. 5 Cross-Training Workouts for Seniors

Strength training becomes even more critical as you age. Here’s how to do it.

If you’ve never prioritized strength training as part of your fitness routine, it’s not too late to start.

A recent study published in the International Journal of Sport Nutrition and Exercise Metabolism recruited two groups of senior participants. Individuals in the first group were between 65 and 75 years old, and those in the second group were 85 years and older. Neither group had engaged in resistance training for at least six months. After following a 12-week strength-training program, both cohorts showed significant improvements in muscle mass, strength, and physical performance.

This doesn’t mean you should wait for your golden years to pick up a dumbbell. Age-related sarcopenia, the loss of muscle mass and function, can begin in your 30s, says Robert Linkul, C.S.C.S., owner of Training The Older Adult. And it only ramps up with every passing decade. “There’s a constant battle against sarcopenia,” he tells Bicycling. “But if you resistance train your entire life, your body shouldn’t change drastically. Naturally, you’ll lose some muscle mass. There’s going to be some degeneration of performance and power output. But as long as you keep trying to maintain it, you’ll have it.”

Julie Logue, M.P.H., senior program manager for Silver Sneakers, agrees that strength training is particularly worthwhile for seniors. “As muscular strength and endurance improves, you can perform activities of daily living with greater ease,” she says, noting that a regular resistance training program can also help older individuals maintain bone density, improve balance, reduce the risk of falling, and correct muscle imbalances. “Because cycling uses some parts of the body more than others, strength training is a necessary complement to promote muscle balance and reduce overuse injuries. Increasing strength can also benefit cyclists by increasing overall endurance and postural control,” she says.

Convinced but not sure where to start? With Linkul’s help, we put together five strength-training workouts you can do on cross-training days. Each one includes senior-appropriate exercises, some of which can be modified or progressed depending on your skill level and experience. For exercises that require added resistance, choose a load that’s heavy but doable; on a scale of 1 to 10, with 10 being your max effort, aim for between a 6 and 7.

Cyclists who are entirely new to strength training want to go lighter at first. “Beginning with bodyweight movements can help build a foundation for using external resistance,” Logue says. She also recommends consulting a primary care provider before starting any new exercise program.

Like most bodyweight workouts, you can do this full-body circuit anywhere, making it a convenient option for when you’re traveling, can’t get to the gym, or just don’t feel like dealing with a bunch of equipment. You’ll work every major muscle group, including your deep core, and train functional, everyday movement patterns, like standing from a sitting position, pushing up from the floor, and maintaining balance and control while stepping backward.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a chair, box, or bench.

Stand in front of a chair, box, or bench with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Tap the chair with glutes. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and body forming straight line from head to feet. Drive right foot to chest. Step back to plank. Repeat on left side. Continue alternating. Do 15 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward. Repeat, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start faceup with arms at sides, legs together, and feet on an elevated surface, like a small box, bench, or chair. Engage core and lift hips off ground so body forms a straight line from heels to shoulders. (Head and shoulders stay on ground, like a straight-leg glute bridge.) Allow arms to rest on ground or, for added difficulty, lift them off floor so elbows are straight and fingertips point up. Hold for 30-60 seconds.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Start in plank position, shoulders over wrists and forming straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows, lowering body to floor while maintaining straight line. Press back up to plank. Repeat. Do 12 reps. Perform on knees or with hands against wall to make it easier.

This workout develops core strength through exercises that challenge your balance and train transferable skills, like carrying a heavy load, crawling in multiple directions, and shifting your body weight from a lying-down position. The single-leg glute bridge and superman variation fire up the posterior chain, which is critical for cyclists, and the three-way toe tap will help improve your overall balance and stability.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and a dumbbell or kettlebell.

Start on hands and knees, shoulders over wrists and knees under hips. Lift knees just about an inch off floor. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the right. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot backward. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot to the left. Take two steps with opposite hand and foot forward. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet together. Send hips back, back flat and core engage, to lower into a shallow hinge position. Keeping weight on left leg, tap right foot forward, then back to left foot. Tap right foot out to the side, then back to left foot. Tap right foot backward, then back to left foot. That’s 1 rep. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists, forming a straight line from head to heels. Tap right hand to left shoulder. Then return to plank. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Holding a dumbbell or kettlebell in one hand, stand tall with shoulders back, chin parallel to the floor, and arms straight down at sides. Keep shoulders over hips (be careful not to lean away from weighted arm) and relax shoulders as you slowly walk forward for 30-60 seconds. Repeat, holding weight on opposite side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted, arms down by sides. Lift and straighten right leg, knees in line. Drive through left foot to lift hips up. Pause, then slowly lower back down. Lift with glutes and hamstrings, rather than low back. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

A dedicated upper-body workout counteracts the time cyclists spend leaning forward in a rounded position and can help correct postural issues, alleviate back pain, and lead to better performance on the bike. This workout includes both pushing and pulling movement patterns and targets the muscles of the chest, back, shoulders, arms, and core.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, and a medicine ball.

Lie faceup on a bench or mat, knees bent and feet planted, holding a dumbbell in each hand, held above shoulders. Slowly lower weights toward chest, bending elbows, with elbows about 45 degrees from torso. Press weights back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg bent or straight (whatever is more comfortable). Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand, arm extended down in front of you. This is the starting position. Row weight to hip by pulling elbow back and keeping it close to side. Keep shoulders down and back, back flat, and core engaged. Extended arm back down slowly to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, knees soft, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders with elbows bent and palms facing each other. Press weights overhead, extending arms. Slowly lower back down to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a staggered stance, left foot forward with knee bent, back right leg straight. Hinge at hips with back flat and core tight. Hold a dumbbell in right hand at hip with elbow bent. This is the starting position. Straighten right arm back behind you, extending elbow. Bend elbow to return to starting position. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart in front of a wall, a little farther than arm’s length away, slight bend in knees, holding a medicine ball at chest. Toss medicine ball toward wall. Catch. Repeat. Do 8 reps.

Strengthening the glutes, hamstrings, quads, and calves can help cyclists unlock (and maintain) the muscular power and endurance needed to tackle hills, power through speed intervals, and resist fatigue on long rides. It can also improve your movement quality off the bike. “A comprehensive lower-body strength and mobility routine can help ensure muscle balance through the low back, hip, and knee, all necessary for maintaining appropriate gait and postural control,” Logue says.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps described, resting 1 minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat, dumbbells, a box, and a hex bar.

Stand inside the hex bar, feet hip-width apart, toes forward. (Or hold a dumbbell in each hand down in front of you.) Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core engaged, shoulders down and back. Lower torso toward floor until parallel or you feel a pull in hamstrings. Maintain a slight bend in knees. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending hips. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, toes turned slightly out. Hold a dumbbell vertically at chest with both hands. Send hips back and down to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Stand behind a step or box, holding a dumbbell in each hand, down by sides. Place right foot on top. Drive through right foot to stand up, extending knee and hips. Drive left knee up to hip height at top. Slowly lower back down. Step off box. Repeat on opposite side. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step out wide with right foot, bend knee, and send hips back, dumbbells framing foot. Keep left leg straight and weight in right heel. Drive through right foot to stand up, foot stepping back to hip-width apart. Repeat, left foot stepping out. Continue alternating. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent and feet planted. Place one or two dumbbells on hips. Drive through feet to lift hips up, engaging glutes, hamstrings, and core. Avoid lifting with lower back. Slowly lower hips back down. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

If you want to capitalize on the benefits of strength training but only have time to train a couple of times a week, this full-body strength workout is the way to go. By incorporating compound movements, you’ll hit every major muscle group with just a handful of exercises.

Perform the following exercises in order for the number of reps indicated, resting one minute between sets. Repeat for a total of 3 rounds.

You will need an exercise mat and dumbbells.

Stand with feet hip-width apart. Lift right heel and line right toes up with left heel. Hold a dumbbell in each hand, down in front of you. This is the starting position. Hinge at hips by sending butt straight back, keeping back flat and core tight. Lower torso toward floor, slight bend in knees, until you feel a pull in hamstrings or torso is parallel to floor. Drive through left foot to stand up, extending hips and returning to starting position. Repeat. Do 10 reps. Then switch sides.

Stand with feet shoulder-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand at shoulders, elbows bent and palms facing each other. Send hips down and back to lower into a squat. Drive through feet to stand back up, extending arms overhead as you stand. Return weights to shoulders. Repeat. Do 12 reps.

Start in a plank position, shoulders over wrists and hands on dumbbells, forming a straight line from head to heels. Bend elbows to lower body to floor for a push-up, maintaining one straight line with body. Press back up. Row right weight to hip, keeping elbow close to side. Place back down. Repeat on left side. That’s 1 rep. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

Stand with feet hip-width apart, holding a dumbbell in each hand down by sides. Step back with right foot, bending both knees 90 degrees; front left knee tracking over toes and back right knee hovering just above floor. Drive through left foot to stand back up, stepping right foot forward, and at the top, curl weights to shoulders, bending elbows. Extend weights back down by sides. Repeat lunge, stepping left foot back. Continue alternating, with biceps curl at the top of each lunge. Do 10 reps per side.

Lie faceup, knees bent, feet planted on the floor. Hold a weight in each hand, then extend arms up, weights over shoulders. Drive through heels, engaging glutes to lift hips up toward the ceiling. Body should form a straight line from shoulders to knees. Pause for a few seconds. Then lower back down slowly, while keeping arms extended. Repeat. Do 10 reps.

#8923. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Marathon

Use walk breaks to finish your first marathon—or even score a BQ.

Completing a marathon sits at the top of many runners’ bucket lists, whether it’s a World Marathon Major with thousands of fellow competitors or a small hometown race. It’s a goal that requires plenty of dedication and consistency—along with hundreds of training miles and regular strength workouts—no matter where you are in your running journey.

But you can make the 26.2-mile distance more manageable with a smarter training and racing strategy: adding short walk breaks into your runs.

Runner’s World’s guide, How to Master the Run/Walk Method, shows you how to successfully navigate marathon training and race day with intentional walk intervals. With the run/walk strategy, you can build your endurance for the marathon distance—while still prioritizing recovery and smarter training.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Train for a Marathon, we’ll teach you:

Training Principles for Consistent Success

Adding walk breaks into your training isn’t reserved for marathon newcomers, nor does it mean you’ll perform slower on race day. It’s a smart strategy runners of all levels can use—and it might even help you go faster than when you’ve previously run a full marathon without stopping.

Using walk intervals as a marathoner could help you:

Boston Marathon on your bucket list? Many run/walkers have earned a coveted Boston qualifying time using strategic walk breaks. “We’ve also talked to plenty of runners who have struggled with breaking a time barrier in the marathon,” says Chris Twiggs, chief training officer at Galloway Training. “But once they tried the run/walk method, they finally hit their goal. And in some cases, that meant earning a BQ.”

The faster you aim to go in your marathon, the shorter your walk breaks and the quicker your run pace. You’ll set your training and race paces using your Magic Mile, multiplying your timed mile by 1.3.

Use one of Runner’s World’s three run/walk plans—beginner, intermediate, and advanced—to tackle the 26.2-mile distance. Across either 20 or 26 weeks, you’ll incorporate run/walk workouts, easy walks, long runs, speed sessions, race pace work, and optional cross-training into your build to prepare your body for the demands of the marathon.

Ideal for: Runners who already do walks or short run/walk workouts and want time to build up their time on feet and endurance for 26.2 miles.

With the beginner plan, you’ll complete two 30-to-45-minute run/walk workouts, an easy walk of 20 to 45 minutes, two optional cross-training days, and a rest day each week. Long runs start at two miles and work up to 26 miles in week 23. Running close to the 26.2-mile distance in training will help your body build endurance and prepare for the demands of the distance ahead of race day.

For your long runs, keep your pace 90 seconds to two minutes slower than your predicted marathon pace. On your cross-training days, you can do strength workouts to build resiliency, or also complete other complementary exercises like cycling or swimming.

Ideal for: Runners who have some racing experience and consistently run/walk three times a week.

This plan follows some of the same training principles as the beginner plan, including two 30-to-45-minute run/walk workouts, two optional cross-training days, an easy walk day, and a rest day. Your long runs begin with five to nine miles and work up to 26 miles by week 17.

Ideal for: Runners who have already completed a marathon and want to finally break through a time barrier or run a new PR. You’ll also want a strong base before hopping into the plan.

Each week of the advanced plan includes two optional cross-training days, a 30-to-45-minute easy run/walk workout, and a rest day. You’ll start with higher mileage for long runs compared to the beginner and intermediate plans, beginning with 12 to 14 miles. You’ll also complete consistent speedwork and race pace miles throughout your marathon build.

One crucial speed workout you’ll grow accustomed to during your training: mile repeats. To complete the workout, you’ll warm up for one mile, then run a mile at a pace 30 seconds per mile faster than your race pace. Afterward, you’ll walk for five minutes and repeat both the quicker mile and the five-minute recovery interval. The number of reps will progress from four to 14 miles. For example, if your marathon race pace is 10 minutes, you’ll run a mile at 9:30 pace, followed by five minutes of walking recovery.

Race pace miles equal running faster than your easy run/walks and long runs. Run at the pace you plan to run on race day and use your goal run/walk ratio.

During your build, you’ll dial in your pacing plan, fueling strategy, and run/walk ratio. You’ll also train yourself to push back against the late-race “wall” of fatigue marathoners often face by completing slow long runs working up to 26 miles. It’s all part of a strong race plan rehearsal meant to help you feel strong come race day. Once you cross that start line, trust all of that training and weeks of practice to propel you to the finish.

One of the most important rules of thumb: Nothing new on race day. Stick with your routine that you built during your training block, and refrain from adding new fuel sources, gear, and pacing strategies to your marathon.

In the first third of the marathon, you should feel relaxed—not huffing and puffing. If you feel like you’re pushing yourself too hard during the first miles, slow down and take more frequent walk breaks. You should save pushing the pace for the very end of your race, and if you conserve your energy early on, you’ll have enough left in the tank to close hard toward the finish.

While time banking for a faster marathon is a myth, energy banking does exist. If you save your energy early on, you’ll likely find that toward the end of your race, you can tap into that energy and finish strong.

Useful, cyclist-approved picks that feel thoughtful without blowing your holiday budget.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. How we test gear.

As a lifelong cyclist, I’ve received well-intentioned bicycle-themed presents that sit around unused, get forgotten in my closet, or are regifted or donated years later. If you’re shopping for a Christmas or birthday gift for a bike rider, buy something they will truly appreciate and actually use.

Admittedly, buying gifts for cyclists isn’t always easy, and every bicycle rider is different. Cycling is often an expensive, gear-heavy activity with many niches and sub-categories, each with particular equipment needs. Resist the temptation to buy a T-shirt with a poorly drawn bike, AI-generated artwork, or a novelty cycling jersey. Instead, choose something they will love. You can find great gifts that show you put in the extra effort, won’t break your budget, or take weeks to arrive.

Here’s a list of 20 of the most helpful, beautiful, fun, and affordable gifts for cyclists under $50; items we’ve tested, loved, and rely on. Want even more great deals on cycling gear and accessories? Bookmark our Best Bike Gear Deals page for sales and discounts from top cycling retailers.

Bells are handy on the bike path, around town, and on the trail. Aussie brand Knog’s Oi bell is discreet, looks good on everything from a commuter to a race bike, and weighs only about 25 grams. Pick up the Oi Classic with a glass-fiber lever or step up to the Oi Luxe with a metal hammer for about $20 more.

Lezyne makes some of our favorite cycling lights for commuting, road, gravel, and mountain biking. However, while super bright and durable, the brand’s lights can be a bit costly. The KTV Drive combo is a lightweight set of front and rear lights to keep riders visible on commutes and in urban environments. They’re rechargeable, have up to 40 hours of runtime, and fit most bikes.

Electric mini inflators have taken the cycling world by storm. These devices let you quickly and precisely air up any bike tire. However, most inflators are a bit too large and heavy to carry in a jersey pocket or seat bag. Although the Pocket SE doesn’t have a pressure gauge, this pint-sized inflator weighs only 90 grams and fills up to four tires per charge.

The Duraglove ETs from Defeet are an awesome addition to any rider’s fall and winter cycling wardrobe. They’re perfect for rides where temperatures are still above freezing but not warm enough to go without gloves. These gloves have rubber grippers (for holding your handlebar in wet conditions) and are touchscreen-compatible with your smartphone or head unit. They’re an excellent value for under $25.

Sometimes the best gifts are high-end versions of normal things you wouldn’t buy for yourself. The design uses nested and flippable magnetic bits made from high-quality stainless steel. As a bonus gift, the Essential8 pairs perfectly with the Coworking5 extension.

The brand’s formula is designed to replace exactly what you lose through heavy sweating, whether riding outdoors or on the indoor trainer. Skratch offers several flavors (like lemon-lime, orange, pineapple, and more) and seasonal ones (like apple cider).

Want to save weight in your tires or space in your seat bag? TPU tubes are lighter than traditional butyl rubber tubes and roll faster. Toe covers are perfect for days when it’s not quite cold enough for full booties, but you want to keep your toes warm on the ride. #8921. Don’t Get Locked Into a Spring or Fall Marathon Cycle. A Run Coach Explains Why You Should Race in Other Seasons.

Here’s how to adjust your training timeline for better weather, faster performances, and more motivation.

We earn a commission for products purchased through some links in this article. Why Trust Us?

When choosing a marathon, most runners focus on the details of the race itself: size, location, weather, elevation, and crowd support. Those are crucial considerations, of course, but they only account for one day, compared with the months you spend training for 26.2 miles. So, you also need to factor in what those months of training could look like depending on the race you choose.

Once you do that, you may realize that racing your marathon in the winter or summer actually benefits you more than racing in the spring or fall. In fact, some runners find that the PRs just out of their reach during those more popular racing windows were simply waiting for them in a different season. The missing piece? Moving the timeline of their marathon cycle to maximize factors like consistency.

A run coach who’s competed in every season explains how to pick a race that sets you up to perform at the right time each year and how flipping your training and racing seasons just might lead to more fun, less stress, and even faster times.

Some of the biggest, most exciting 26.2s occur in the fall and spring—take six of the World Majors, for example. But these marathons can also come with less-than-ideal training timelines, Elizabeth Corkum, a.k.a. Coach Corky, an RRCA-, UESCA-, and USATF-certified run coach, tells Runner’s World.

When race day falls in September, October, or April, you’ll likely have your most important workouts and long runs on tap for the least ideal weather of the summer and winter months: brutal heat and humidity or short days with ice and cold temperatures, Corkum explains. Many runners, though, deem these tougher training conditions a fair trade for a shot at a cool, dry day in the low 50s when they toe the starting line.

Some runners would rather flip the script: Do the bulk of their training and peak mileage weeks in nicer weather, instead of hoping for ideal conditions on race day.

If you don’t enjoy running as much when you’re waking up at 4 a.m. in the summer to beat the heat or waiting until the sun goes down to squeeze in miles just before bed, you may benefit from switching your main training season. Some options to consider might be the California International Marathon (CIM) in December or the Houston Marathon in January, Corkum suggests.

Or, maybe you find yourself worn down from trudging through sleet and slush, bundling up for runs in below-freezing temps, logging miles in the dark when the days shorten, or simply confining yourself to the treadmill because it’s the only place that isn’t slick with ice. In that case, you might want to complete your heaviest training in the spring for a summer race. Some great options to consider are Grandma’s Marathon in June, the San Francisco Marathon in July, and the Gold Coast Marathon in July.

For many runners, the greatest benefit of doing the bulk of their training during the fall and spring is that they enjoy the process more. They’re excited to get out the door each day to put in the miles when the weather is cool and crisp from September through November, or they’re finally catching glimpses of green and spring blooms from March through May.

“The mental impact of just grinding day after day in the bitter cold or brutal heat can sometimes make running feel less fun, and I think there is some mental exhaustion that can come from doing that in summer and winter,” Corkum says. “Some people love it and they thrive on it—but many don’t.”

When runners can train in the conditions they feel their best in, they’re usually able to get their miles in more consistently and the entire marathon cycle becomes more enjoyable, she adds.

Once you make the switch, you may not only find that it’s less challenging for you to adhere to your training schedule but that you also have more mental energy and motivation. While these benefits are psychological, they can lead to real physiological training improvements, too.

Besides the mental boost that comes from logging miles in the spring and fall, you might find that your body responds better to training in milder conditions, as well. This may allow you to train harder and recover more quickly.

“October and November are months during which I sweat less and running is not as taxing,” Corkum says. “My heart rate is 5, 10, even 15 beats lower at the same effort because of the weather. And because of that, all my easy runs are even easier on my body.”

Corkum has found that she can usually handle about 10 to 15 more miles each week, and this higher training load, for her, doesn’t require as much recovery as it would during the hotter months of the year. “There’s a huge benefit if we can add more mileage with less stress on the body. If we’re able to run more, that can make us much better runners,” she explains.

A study of more than 119,000 runners published in Sports Medicine in 2024 backs up Corkum’s recommendation: Higher averages of easy-running mileage were associated with faster race performances. So consider which season allows you to safely and comfortably log more miles each week.

Regardless of the season you choose for your marathon, good weather isn’t guaranteed. Corkum says runners should prepare for the possibility that even races like CIM, which has a strong track record for being cool and overcast, could experience an unexpected pop of heat. So, she encourages runners to incorporate some type of heat training—especially if you’re not getting much exposure to hot and humid temps during runs.

“We don’t need to be running in uncomfortably hot and humid conditions every single day to be ready for a warmer race day. Passive heat training—sitting in a hot tub, bathtub, steam room, or sauna—can help us heat adapt, too,” Corkum says.

Another tip Corkum gives her athletes? Do your research. “Go online to check the average temperatures and dew points of a race for the last 10 years or so. Look at the outliers, too,” she says. This information helps you determine if race day and the training season will offer the conditions you want.

And finally, learn to adapt when—despite your best preparations—race day doesn’t go your way. Ask yourself how you’ll adjust your expectations, fueling, and pacing instead of forcing the effort, because that can change your experience of the day and even your finish time, Corkum says.

The season for your best marathon performance will largely depend on your ability to prioritize the aspects of training and racing that feel most important to you, Corkum explains. So when choosing your marathon, consider how much emphasis you’re putting on both race day and the months of the journey.

“Of course, we all want the perfect day for our marathon. But it’s the months of training beforehand that get us there feeling fit and confident,” she says. Keeping both pieces in mind can help ease race-day pressure and elevate your entire marathon cycle regardless of the time of year—or time on the finish clock.

Morgan is a gear editor who has been with Runner’s World since 2017. She started as an intern ghostwriting The Warmup, a bygone version of the daily RW newsletter. Now, she tests and reviews anything you might find on runners’ feet-from crew socks and compression boots to carbon-plated super shoes.

A lifelong runner and shoe geek, Morgan has been chasing the perfect pair of kicks since she joined her grade school cross-country team. Since then, she ran as a Division I walk-on for the cross-country and track & field teams at the University of Delaware, where she studied English and Biology. She has one full marathon under her belt, and has raced more halfs and 5Ks than she can count.

#8920. I Got Shingles Training for a Marathon. I’m Not the Only One.

Shingles typically appears as a band of blistering, painful rash on one side of the body. (Photo: Getty Images)

I had just finished the last hard training run of my marathon build, 19 miles with 15 at race pace. I nailed it, but couldn’t help thinking it felt harder than it should have.

“It’s just nerves,” I told myself. “You’ll have two weeks to taper, and you’ll be ready to run that BQ (Boston Marathon Qualifying time) on race day.”

The next day, I felt exhausted, and my ribs were sore and tender to the touch. I started to wonder if I’d pulled a muscle in my rib cage while breathing heavily during my training run. I, of course, turned to Google. “Ribs sore from running.” “Ribs hurt after running.” Most of the posts advised that I’d feel better in a day.

But I didn’t feel better the next day. Instead, I noticed a small pink mark on my stomach, and now my ribs felt both sore and tingly. My Google searches grew more alarming: I could have shingles.

I scheduled an appointment for that same day, and my doctor confirmed it. She took one look at me and said, “I’m so sorry, you have shingles.”

Shingles is a painful viral infection that looks like a terrible rash and usually involves nerve pain that can last for months. The virus comes from dormant chickenpox in your body that can reappear when you’re stressed.

My doctor asked about stressors in my life. “I haven’t really been that stressed,” I promised, saying my family life and my career were extremely smooth. “But I have been training for a marathon,” I said.

“That could do it,” she told me. “Your body is clearly telling you that you were pushing too hard.”

I’m 43, younger than the typical shingles patient, but I’m part of an unfortunate trend. Shingles cases are on the rise and the biggest increase is among people in their 30s and 40s. One study found overall shingles cases nearly doubled between 2005 and 2021. Another found cases in Americans under 50 quadrupled from the late 1940s to 2000, and are still going up, according to data from the CDC.

A big reason for the increase among millennials is that we fall into a gap: 50 and up, and you can get the shingles vaccine; 30 and under, and you’ve had the chickenpox vaccine, which will make getting shingles way less likely.

That age range is also most common among marathoners, so my big question was whether running, especially hard training, can give you shingles. Unfortunately, that specific question hasn’t been extensively studied, so there’s no clear-cut answer. But doctors are drawing correlations between heavy training and whether it decreases the body’s immunity overall.

There’s research that shows immunity dips after heavy training, says David Nieman, DrPH, FACSM, director of the Human Performance Laboratory at Appalachian State University. He pointed to a study involving mice and the herpes virus.

“When you infected the mice and then forced them to run to exhaustion, there was a higher mortality rate in those mice than mice that just did moderate activity and rested,” he says. “Moderate activity actually helped a little bit, but by far the really bad response was in the mice that ran to exhaustion.”

In another study, researchers gave horses the flu and then ran them really hard. Those horses developed a longer-lasting, more intense bout of the flu compared to the horses who were infected but didn’t run hard, he said.

But Nieman and other researchers agree that moderate exercise can actually boost your immunity. James Turner, a professor at the Sport, Exercise and Rehabilitation Sciences school at the University of Birmingham, says it’s far more common that inadequate sleep, diet and psychological stress suppress immunity than exercise, even really hard training.

“Research on both prolonged exercise and marathon running shows that antibody responses are not suppressed and might actually be higher,” he says.

Meanwhile, Dr. William Schaffner, MD, a professor of infectious diseases at Vanderbilt Health who’s an expert in shingles, says it’s too soon to say definitely that lots of stress leads to the virus. He points out there’s no evidence that soldiers in combat or police and firefighters have an increased risk of shingles.

“When people get a shingles episode, there is a tendency to look back in their lives to see if there might be some sort of inciting event or stressful event and there’s a tendency to link the two,” he says. “But the question is, is that just coincidence because there’s a lot of stress in life, or was it a causal relationship? I think we’ll still have to say that hasn’t been definitively settled.”

Instead, for Schaffner, the likeliest explanation for the increase in shingles is because the chickenpox vaccine is decreasing our exposure to chickenpox. We used to all get chickenpox as children, and so the virus was more common in the wild. That gave our immune systems a boost. Now that there’s a vaccine, that isn’t happening, which means we may be more likely to get shingles, he said.

Whether my running caused my shingles or not, as soon as I had my diagnosis, my next questions were about my marathon. My doctor said my symptoms would likely peak in four days to a week, and so it still seemed possible I would be ready for race day. I rushed out to get a seven-day course of Valtrex—if you start an antiviral treatment quickly enough, it can stop the spread of the shingles rash.

But as the week passed and the rash grew along my rib cage to my back, it only continued to feel worse. I was achy everywhere, and my ribs felt like they were constantly being stabbed with tiny needles. A week later, I called it and canceled my marathon plans, harboring a hope that within a few weeks I would be better and could rebound to run my BQ.

What I did next probably hurt my cause rather than helped it. As soon as I felt a bit better, I would go out and do a race-pace run, which would give me a painful setback that lasted for several days. This likely was making my bout with the virus longer, Nieman says.

He reminded me of the mice who were running to exhaustion and not getting well. The mice really needed to keep it low-key to get an immune boost, not drain.

“If they did 30 minutes of something like a brisk walk equivalent, that would help a little bit,” he says.

My conversation with him sounded like a negotiation.

“I’m mostly feeling better, but I still sometimes have sensations in my ribs, so do I still need to take it easy?” I asked.

“I have a lot of empathy. I know you don’t want to hear it,” he said gently. Nieman has run 58 marathons himself, so he knows the feeling. “You don’t want anybody telling you not to run, but this is where you’ve got to be really, really careful and just bide your time and slowly get back into it once you feel better.”

His advice to runners: listen to your body and don’t push yourself. That’s not an easy metric for marathoners who are used to pushing beyond what feels comfortable, but Nieman says exhaustion can exacerbate the nerve pain and make it all last much longer.

Other things to keep in mind: it’s possible that sunburns can impede your immune system, so cover up once you’re back out and running, says Jennifer Moffat, a SUNY microbiology and immunology professor and expert on chickenpox and shingles.

And, Moffat says, while you still have a rash, you’re contagious and can spread the virus to others through contact. If you’re at the gym or anywhere you might touch other people, you should have the rash fully covered.

She also advises keeping an eye on the other stresses around marathons, like not eating enough, not sleeping enough, and the mental stress around races.

“The anticipation, logistics, travel hassles, changes in environment and food, rivalries with other competitors, jet lag, time away from family, the cost can become overwhelming,” she says. “Getting to the starting line of a marathon is much more than showing up with your shoes tied.”

In fact, she says, it’s common for people to come down with other viral infections right before a race (the dreaded taper cold).

As for me, two months after my rash first appeared, I finally truly threw in the towel. I couldn’t keep up any kind of marathon training without making myself feel worse, so I switched to low-effort maintenance running and decided my BQ would have to come next year.

#8919. How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Training Principles for Consistent Success

Build a well-rounded run/walk routine with these tips from experts.

Whether you want to boost your health, run your first race, or set a new PR, the run/walk method makes those goals accessible for everyone of all fitness backgrounds and levels. But finding run/walk success goes well beyond determining your Magic Mile paces, tracking your intervals, and finishing your goal race.

By following some key training principles, you can make your run/walk regimen a fundamental part of your everyday routine. Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method program walks you through the essential guidance you need to stick with your training, stay healthy, and enjoy each step of your run/walk journey.

In Runner’s World’s How to Master the Run/Walk Method: Training Principles for Consistent Success, we’ll teach you:

As you continue with your run/walk routine and watch your training progress, keep the following training principles in mind for long-term run/walk success:

Practice makes perfect, right? Training on a regular basis—even when you’re not working toward a goal race—will help you reach your fitness aims and maintain your run/walk progress.

Now, that doesn’t mean you need to be in race training mode year round. Use one of Runner’s World’s maintenance plans to structure your off-season workouts and sustain your motivation. You can also use our four-week run/walk maintenance plan, which keeps your body prepped before heading into your next training cycle.

All of our run/walk training plans have a weekly rest day for a reason. The time you spend off your feet is when progress happens, allowing your body to soak up all of the hard work you’ve put in. Build in recovery time after your hard workouts and long runs, and also set aside a few minutes each day for recovery methods like stretching or foam rolling.

And don’t forget to catch those z’s! Sleep is one of—if not the—most important recovery tools you can use to your advantage for muscle and tissue repair, improved immune function, and injury prevention, among other benefits.

While it’s important to stay consistent with your running mileage, it’s also important to strength train. We recommend adding strength training into your routine one to three times a week to support stronger muscles, protect your joints, add force behind your stride, and become more resilient.

Aim for more strength workouts earlier in your training block. As your mileage and workout intensity increases throughout your plan, you can reduce your strength workout frequency.

Not sure where to begin with strength workouts? Use our Guide to Strength Training and Race-Ready Strength program to get started with your routine.

A smart nutrition strategy keeps you running strong, and is an especially important consideration as you start running longer distances like half marathons and marathons. As you increase your activity, your body needs more calories to support that movement.

To build your runner’s diet, prioritize whole foods, along with grains, fruits, vegetables, and lean proteins in your diet. Make sure to hydrate, both throughout your day and during your workouts, with water and electrolytes to replenish fluids.

Before long runs, eat enough carbohydrates, and get a good mix of carbs and protein into your system afterward. For runs longer than 60 minutes, bring fuel with you, like gels, gummies, electrolytes, and sports drinks.

For more on how to properly fuel your training and racing, dig into the Runner’s World Guide to Nutrition and Fueling, which includes tips from industry experts on hydration, midrun fueling, race day nutrition, and so much more.

Running is often seen as a solo sport—but it doesn’t have to be. Find a run club, virtual run/walk group, or a training partner to stay consistent with your training and have fun while doing so. Having other run/walkers supporting you helps you stay accountable, find meaning in your miles, and unlock even more enjoyment.

“The fact of the matter is running is a lot more fun when you’re doing it with other people,” says experienced run/walker Cheryl Munn. “I don’t think that I would’ve kept at it if I hadn’t joined a local running group.”

Ashley is Editor of Content Hype at Hearst’s Enthusiast & Wellness Group. She is a former collegiate runner at UNC Asheville where she studied mass communication. Ashley loves all things running; she has raced two marathons, plus has covered some of the sport’s top events in her career, including the Paris Olympics, U.S. Olympic Trials and multiple World Marathon Majors.

#8917. 10-Minute Morning Yoga for Strength and Surrender

Gillian E. Boult is a yoga teacher, registered social worker, psychotherapist, and author. Also an avid hiker and explorer, Gillian brings her mat into diverse landscapes, using nature as a co-regulator to soothe the nervous system, release tension, and restore cognitive focus. Here, she shares a flow in front of a waterfall.

Adding yoga to your morning routine is among the best ways to set the tone for your day. While most mornings are jammed with to-dos and getting ready rituals, taking even a few minutes to roll out your mat teaches your body, breath, and mind that presence and peace are the priority.

This 10-minute yoga practice encourages you to channel the energy of a waterfall—powerful and ever-shifting—beginning your day with strength and surrender. A series of side and forward bends, core-engaging shapes, and lower body stretches wakes up your body while reminding you of its inherent vitality.

No props are needed for this practice—just your body, your breath, and (if available) a jaw-dropping natural backdrop. If you don’t have access to nature, close your eyes when you flow allows and picture yourself in the outdoor space of your dreams, complete with sound.

Begin in a comfortable seated position, such as Easy Pose, rooting down through your sit bones. Rest your hands in your lap and either close your eyes or soften your gaze.

On your next inhalation, sweep both arms overhead and reach tall. Exhale as you take a side bend toward the left, reaching your right arm overhead as you release your left fingertips, hand, or forearm to the ground.

Inhale to come back through center. Extend your right leg out long and center your chest and hips so you’re facing your right foot. With your exhalation, hinge forward in Head-to-Knee Forward Bend, reaching any amount and resting your hands on your calf, ankle, or foot. Feel free to bend your right knee if that’s more comfortable for you.

Inhale to lift your torso, then plant your left hand behind your left hip, pressing into that hand and engaging your hips to lift in a kneeling variation of Wild Thing.

Exhale to release down to your left side body. Rest on your forearm, stack your knees, and use your right hand in front of you for support as you extend your right leg toward the sky. You might want to grab hold of your right foot or leg in this variation of Reclining Hand-to-Big-Toe.

Release your foot, slowly lowering it all the way to the ground and press through its outer edge. Inhale as you press into your left forearm and lift yourself off the mat while reaching your right arm toward the sky in a variation of Side Plank. Option to bend your bottom knee as you bring your foot behind your or to reach your top arm alongside your head.

When you’re ready, lower down to Easy Pose. Repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

With your exhalation lower down and come to a seat. Extend your legs out wide. Grow tall with your inhalation and exhale into Wide-Angled Seated Forward Bend, hinging at your hips and walking your hands forward any amount that is comfortable.

When you’re ready, walk your hands back in and carefully come onto all fours in a Tabletop position.

Once you’re settled in Tabletop, lift your right leg and guide your knee through 3 large hip circles.

Step your right foot through to land between the hands. On an inhalation, reach your arms overhead and sink deeper into your Low Lunge.

With your next exhalation, bring your hands to the mat and tuck your back toes under, straightening your right left and shifting your sit bones back in Half Splits.

When you’re ready, come back to Tabletop and repeat the following poses on the opposite side:

Come back through Tabletop and widen your knees. Touch your toes together and sink your hips back in Child’s Pose. Notice how you feel in your body here, maybe setting an intention for the rest of your day. Let a word come to you.

Stay here for 1-3 minutes or as long as you’d like.

Once you feel complete, press up to kneel in Thunderbolt Pose. Inhale your arms up overhead, and exhale to bring your hands together at heart center.

Thank yourself for taking the time to make it to your mat today.
